topic: LTI behaviour: impulse response, convolution, frequency response
stem: The convolution of two rectangular pulses of equal width \(T\) gives:
explanation: Convolving identical rectangles produces a triangle of double the duration.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 1

topic: LTI behaviour: impulse response, convolution, frequency response
stem: Convolution of \(x(t)\) with \(\delta(t-t_0)\) gives:
explanation: Convolving with a shifted impulse simply shifts the signal.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 1

topic: LTI behaviour: impulse response, convolution, frequency response
stem: The step response of an LTI system is related to the impulse response by:
options: It is the convolution of h with itself
It is the derivative of h(t)
It is the running integral of the impulse response
explanation: s(t) = integral of h(tau) d(tau) from -infinity to t.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 1

topic: LTI behaviour: impulse response, convolution, frequency response
stem: When a complex exponential e^{jwt} is applied to an LTI system, the output is:
explanation: Complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of LTI systems; H(jw) is the eigenvalue.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 1

topic: LTI behaviour: impulse response, convolution, frequency response
stem: A sinusoidal input to a stable LTI system produces a steady-state output that is:
options: A sinusoid of the same frequency with altered amplitude and phase
explanation: LTI systems cannot create new frequency components.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 1

topic: LTI behaviour: impulse response, convolution, frequency response
stem: The frequency response of a system is related to the impulse response by:
options: The convolution of h with itself
The Laplace transform of the step response
explanation: H(jw) = F{h(t)}; magnitude and phase give amplitude and phase distortion.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 1

topic: State space representation and state transition matrix
stem: A state-space model of a continuous LTI system is written as:
explanation: The state vector captures the internal memory of the system.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 1

topic: State space representation and state transition matrix
stem: The state transition matrix of a continuous system is:
explanation: It propagates the initial state forward in time in the unforced system.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 1

topic: State space representation and state transition matrix
stem: For a MIMO system with p inputs and q outputs, the transfer function is:
options: A \(q\times p\) matrix of transfer functions
explanation: Each entry relates one input to one output.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 1

topic: State space representation and state transition matrix
stem: A discrete-time state model x[n+1] = Gx[n] + Hu[n] is stable if the eigenvalues of G:
explanation: Discrete modes lambda^n decay only when |lambda| < 1.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 1

topic: System properties: linearity, shift-invariance, causality, stability
stem: Every causal system is necessarily stable.
explanation: Causality and stability are independent; a causal system can have an unbounded impulse response.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 1

topic: LTI behaviour: impulse response, convolution, frequency response
stem: Convolution in the time domain corresponds to multiplication in the frequency domain.
explanation: This is the convolution theorem, the basis of frequency-domain filtering.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 1

topic: LTI behaviour: impulse response, convolution, frequency response
stem:
Assertion (A): Complex exponentials are called eigenfunctions of LTI systems.
Reason (R): The response of an LTI system to a complex exponential is the same exponential scaled by a complex constant.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Only amplitude and phase change, which is precisely the eigenfunction property.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 1

topic: Signal properties and special signals
stem:
Assertion (A): A discrete-time sinusoid is always periodic.
Reason (R): Continuous-time sinusoids are periodic for every frequency.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Discrete sinusoids are periodic only when the normalised frequency is rational.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 1

topic: System properties: linearity, shift-invariance, causality, stability
stem: Which properties does the system \(y[n]=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{n}x[k]\) (accumulator) possess?
explanation: The accumulator is linear, time-invariant and causal, but a bounded step input gives an unbounded ramp output.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 1

topic: Fourier series of periodic signals and waveform symmetry
stem: A periodic signal can be represented by a Fourier series provided it satisfies:
explanation: Finite maxima/minima, finite discontinuities and absolute integrability over one period.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier series of periodic signals and waveform symmetry
stem: The exponential Fourier series of a periodic signal uses basis functions:
explanation: Harmonically related complex exponentials form an orthogonal basis over one period.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier series of periodic signals and waveform symmetry
stem: For a signal with even symmetry, the trigonometric Fourier series contains:
options: Only cosine terms (and a DC term)
explanation: Even symmetry makes all b_n coefficients vanish.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier series of periodic signals and waveform symmetry
stem: A signal with odd symmetry has a Fourier series containing:
options: Only sine terms with zero DC value
explanation: Odd symmetry forces a_0 and all a_n to be zero.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier series of periodic signals and waveform symmetry
stem: A signal with half-wave symmetry contains:
explanation: x(t) = -x(t + T/2) eliminates the DC component and all even harmonics.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier series of periodic signals and waveform symmetry
stem: The DC term a_0 of a Fourier series equals:
options: The average value of the signal over one period
explanation: a_0 = (1/T) times the integral of x(t) over one period.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier series of periodic signals and waveform symmetry
stem: A square wave of amplitude A and 50% duty cycle has harmonic amplitudes falling as:
explanation: Half-wave symmetry removes even harmonics; odd harmonic amplitudes are 4A/(n pi).
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier series of periodic signals and waveform symmetry
stem: The Gibbs phenomenon refers to:
options: Overshoot of about 9% near a discontinuity that persists as more terms are added
explanation: The overshoot narrows but its peak amplitude does not diminish with more harmonics.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier series of periodic signals and waveform symmetry
stem: The Fourier series coefficients of a real-valued signal satisfy:
explanation: Hence the magnitude spectrum is even and the phase spectrum is odd.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier transform, properties and duality
stem: The Fourier transform of a unit impulse delta(t) is:
explanation: An impulse contains all frequencies with equal magnitude.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier transform, properties and duality
stem: The Fourier transform of a rectangular pulse is:
explanation: Rectangle and sinc form a Fourier transform pair, illustrating time-frequency duality.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier transform, properties and duality
stem: Compressing a signal in time by a factor a (a > 1) causes its spectrum to:
options: Expand in frequency by the same factor with reduced amplitude
explanation: The time-scaling property: x(at) transforms to (1/|a|)X(jw/a).
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier transform, properties and duality
stem: A time shift of t0 in a signal causes its Fourier transform to be multiplied by:
explanation: Magnitude spectrum is unaffected; only a linear phase term is added.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier transform, properties and duality
stem: Multiplication of two signals in the time domain corresponds in frequency to:
options: Convolution of their spectra (with a 1/2pi factor)
explanation: This is the dual of the convolution theorem and explains modulation sidebands.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier transform, properties and duality
stem: The frequency-shifting (modulation) property states that multiplying x(t) by e^{jw0 t}:
explanation: This is the basis of amplitude modulation in communication systems.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier transform, properties and duality
stem: Differentiation of x(t) in time corresponds in the frequency domain to:
explanation: Differentiation emphasises high frequencies, hence its noise-amplifying nature.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier transform, properties and duality
stem: Fourier duality implies that if x(t) transforms to X(jw), then X(t) transforms to:
explanation: The symmetric structure of forward and inverse transforms produces this duality.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier transform, properties and duality
stem: The magnitude spectrum of a real signal is always:
explanation: Conjugate symmetry X(-jw) = X*(jw) makes |X| even and the phase odd.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier transform, properties and duality
stem: The Fourier transform of e^{-at}u(t) with a > 0 is:
explanation: A first-order low-pass characteristic with a 3 dB frequency of a rad/s.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier transform, properties and duality
stem: A distortionless transmission system must have:
options: Constant magnitude response and linear phase over the signal band
explanation: Linear phase corresponds to a pure time delay, which does not distort the waveform.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: DTFT, DFT and Parseval's theorem
stem: The DTFT of a discrete-time sequence is:
options: A continuous and periodic function of frequency with period 2 pi
explanation: Sampling in time forces periodicity in the frequency domain.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: DTFT, DFT and Parseval's theorem
stem: The N-point DFT of a sequence x[n] is defined as:
explanation: It samples the DTFT at N equally spaced frequencies around the unit circle.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: DTFT, DFT and Parseval's theorem
stem: The DFT is obtained from the DTFT by:
options: Taking the magnitude of the DTFT
Sampling the DTFT at N uniformly spaced frequencies
explanation: Frequency sampling implies periodic extension of the sequence in the time domain.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: DTFT, DFT and Parseval's theorem
stem: An N-point DFT gives a frequency resolution of:
explanation: Resolution improves by taking more samples, not merely by zero padding.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: DTFT, DFT and Parseval's theorem
stem: A 1024-point DFT of a signal sampled at 8 kHz gives a bin spacing of:
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: DTFT, DFT and Parseval's theorem
stem: Multiplication of two DFTs corresponds in the time domain to:
explanation: Zero padding is used to make circular convolution match linear convolution.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: DTFT, DFT and Parseval's theorem
stem: Linear convolution of sequences of length L and M requires a DFT size of at least:
explanation: Otherwise time-domain aliasing corrupts the circular convolution result.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: DTFT, DFT and Parseval's theorem
stem: Parseval's theorem for the Fourier transform states that:
options: Total energy in time equals total energy in frequency (with a 1/2pi factor)
explanation: It expresses conservation of energy across the transform.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: DTFT, DFT and Parseval's theorem
stem: Parseval's relation for the Fourier series relates average power to:
options: The sum of squared magnitudes of all the Fourier coefficients
explanation: Total average power equals the sum of the powers of the individual harmonics.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: DTFT, DFT and Parseval's theorem
stem: Spectral leakage in the DFT occurs because:
options: The finite observation window truncates the signal, producing sidelobes
explanation: Windowing functions such as Hamming or Hann reduce sidelobe leakage.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: DTFT, DFT and Parseval's theorem
stem: Zero padding a sequence before the DFT:
options: Interpolates the spectrum but does not improve true resolution
explanation: It gives a denser sampling of the same underlying DTFT.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier transform, properties and duality
stem: The Fourier transform of a constant DC signal of amplitude A is:
explanation: A DC signal has all its energy concentrated at zero frequency.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier series of periodic signals and waveform symmetry
stem: The Fourier series of a periodic signal has a spectrum that is:
options: Discrete, existing only at harmonic frequencies
explanation: Periodicity in time produces a line (discrete) spectrum in frequency.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: DTFT, DFT and Parseval's theorem
stem: The DFT assumes the finite-length sequence is periodically extended.
explanation: This implicit periodicity is why DFT multiplication gives circular rather than linear convolution.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier series of periodic signals and waveform symmetry
stem: The Gibbs phenomenon disappears if enough Fourier series terms are used.
explanation: The overshoot narrows but its magnitude remains about 9% of the jump height.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier transform, properties and duality
stem:
Assertion (A): The Fourier transform of a rectangular pulse extends over infinite frequency.
Reason (R): A time-limited signal cannot be band-limited.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Strict time limitation and strict band limitation are mutually exclusive properties.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: DTFT, DFT and Parseval's theorem
stem:
Assertion (A): Zero padding improves the frequency resolution of a DFT.
Reason (R): Zero padding increases the number of DFT points.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: More points only interpolate the spectrum; true resolution needs a longer observation of the signal.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Fourier series of periodic signals and waveform symmetry
stem: Which statements about a periodic square wave with half-wave symmetry are correct?
explanation: Half-wave symmetry removes the DC and even harmonics; odd harmonic amplitudes fall as 1/n.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 2

topic: Laplace transform of continuous signals and systems
stem: The bilateral Laplace transform of x(t) is defined as:
explanation: The unilateral version integrates from 0- and suits causal signals with initial conditions.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace transform of continuous signals and systems
stem: The Laplace transform of e^{-at}u(t) is:
explanation: A single pole at s = -a with region of convergence to the right of the pole.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace transform of continuous signals and systems
stem: The Laplace transform of sin(wt)u(t) is:
explanation: The cosine pair has s in the numerator instead of omega.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace transform of continuous signals and systems
stem: The Laplace transform of t u(t) is:
explanation: Repeated integration of the step gives higher-order poles at the origin.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace transform of continuous signals and systems
stem: The time-differentiation property of the unilateral Laplace transform is:
explanation: Initial conditions enter naturally, which is why Laplace suits circuit transient analysis.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace transform of continuous signals and systems
stem: The Laplace transform of the integral of x(t) from 0 to t is:
explanation: Integration in time corresponds to division by s.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace transform of continuous signals and systems
stem: The region of convergence of a right-sided signal is:
options: To the right of the rightmost pole
To the left of the leftmost pole
explanation: Left-sided signals converge to the left; two-sided signals give a strip.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace transform of continuous signals and systems
stem: A causal LTI system is stable if and only if the ROC:
options: Includes the jw axis, i.e. all poles are in the left half plane
explanation: Only then does the Fourier transform exist and h(t) remain absolutely integrable.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace transform of continuous signals and systems
stem: Applying the shifting property, the Laplace transform of x(t - a)u(t - a) is:
explanation: Time delay corresponds to multiplication by a decaying exponential in s.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace transform of continuous signals and systems
stem: Multiplying x(t) by e^{-at} corresponds in the s-domain to:
explanation: Frequency shifting (the s-shift property) moves all poles by -a.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: System functions, poles and zeros
stem: The system function H(s) of an LTI system is:
options: The Laplace transform of the impulse response
explanation: H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) with zero initial conditions.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: System functions, poles and zeros
stem: The poles of a system function are:
options: Values of s where H(s) becomes infinite (roots of the denominator)
explanation: They determine the natural response modes and stability of the system.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: System functions, poles and zeros
stem: The zeros of a system function are:
options: Roots of the numerator polynomial where H(s) = 0
explanation: Zeros shape the magnitude response but do not affect stability.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: System functions, poles and zeros
stem: A pair of complex conjugate poles at -a +/- jb corresponds to a time-domain mode:
explanation: The real part sets the decay rate and the imaginary part the oscillation frequency.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: System functions, poles and zeros
stem: A pole in the right half s-plane implies:
options: An exponentially growing response, hence instability
explanation: e^{+at} grows without bound, so the system is unstable.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: System functions, poles and zeros
stem: A non-minimum phase system is one with:
options: One or more zeros in the right half s-plane
explanation: Such systems often show an initial undershoot and have extra phase lag.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: System functions, poles and zeros
stem: An all-pass system has:
options: Poles and zeros mirror-imaged about the jw axis, giving constant magnitude
explanation: It alters phase only, and is used as a phase equaliser.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: System functions, poles and zeros
stem: The frequency response is obtained from H(s) by substituting s = jw only when:
options: The ROC includes the jw axis
explanation: Otherwise the Fourier transform of the impulse response does not converge.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: System functions, poles and zeros
stem: Graphically, |H(jw)| at a frequency w can be evaluated as:
options: Product of distances from the zeros divided by product of distances from the poles
explanation: A pole close to the jw axis produces a peak in the magnitude response.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace domain analysis and solution of differential equations
stem: The complete response of a system in the Laplace domain is the sum of:
explanation: Initial conditions produce the zero-input part; the input produces the zero-state part.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace domain analysis and solution of differential equations
stem: Partial fraction expansion is used in Laplace analysis to:
options: Decompose Y(s) into simple terms for easy inverse transformation
explanation: Each simple term corresponds to a standard time-domain function.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace domain analysis and solution of differential equations
stem: For a repeated pole of order 2 at s = -a, the corresponding time function includes:
explanation: Higher-order poles introduce polynomial-in-t multipliers.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace domain analysis and solution of differential equations
stem: The initial value theorem for the Laplace transform states x(0+) equals:
explanation: It is valid when X(s) is a proper rational function.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace domain analysis and solution of differential equations
stem: The final value theorem may be applied only if:
options: All poles of sX(s) lie strictly in the left half plane
explanation: Otherwise the limit does not exist and the theorem gives a misleading answer.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace domain analysis and solution of differential equations
stem: For \(Y(s)=\frac{10}{s(s+5)}\), the final value of y(t) is:
explanation: lim s->0 of sY(s) = 10/5 = 2.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace domain analysis and solution of differential equations
stem: Solving a linear differential equation using Laplace transforms converts it into:
explanation: This is the key computational advantage of the transform method.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace domain analysis and solution of differential equations
stem: In circuit analysis, an inductor with initial current I0 is modelled in the s-domain by:
options: Impedance \(sL\) in series with a voltage source \(LI_0\)
explanation: The initial condition appears as an equivalent independent source.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace domain analysis and solution of differential equations
stem: In the s-domain, a capacitor with initial voltage V0 is represented by:
options: Impedance \(1/sC\) in series with a source \(V_0/s\)
explanation: Alternatively, 1/sC in parallel with a current source CV0.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace domain analysis and solution of differential equations
stem: The natural response of a system is determined by:
options: The zeros of the system function
The poles of the system function
explanation: The forced response terms follow the poles of the input transform.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace domain analysis and solution of differential equations
stem: Resonance in the forced response occurs when:
options: A pole of the input coincides with a pole of the system function
explanation: The repeated pole generates a t-multiplied growing term.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: System functions, poles and zeros
stem: Pole-zero cancellation in H(s) can be problematic because:
options: The cancelled mode still exists internally and may be unstable
explanation: An unstable hidden mode is neither controllable nor observable but still grows.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace transform of continuous signals and systems
stem: Convolution in time corresponds in the Laplace domain to:
explanation: Y(s) = H(s)X(s), which is why transform analysis simplifies LTI problems.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace transform of continuous signals and systems
stem: The Laplace transform is a generalisation of the Fourier transform because:
options: It uses the complex variable \(s=\sigma+j\omega\) rather than only \(j\omega\)
explanation: The sigma factor allows transformation of signals that grow with time.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: System functions, poles and zeros
stem: The location of zeros affects the stability of an LTI system.
explanation: Stability depends only on pole locations; zeros shape the response magnitude and phase.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace transform of continuous signals and systems
stem: The region of convergence must be specified for a bilateral Laplace transform to be unique.
explanation: The same algebraic expression can correspond to different signals with different ROCs.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Laplace domain analysis and solution of differential equations
stem:
Assertion (A): The unilateral Laplace transform is preferred for circuit transient analysis.
Reason (R): It incorporates initial conditions directly through the differentiation property.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Initial capacitor voltages and inductor currents appear naturally as equivalent sources.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: System functions, poles and zeros
stem:
Assertion (A): A system with a pole on the imaginary axis is BIBO stable.
Reason (R): Poles on the imaginary axis produce sustained oscillations.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A bounded sinusoidal input at that frequency gives an unbounded output, so it is not BIBO stable.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: System functions, poles and zeros
stem: Which statements about a causal LTI system with H(s) = (s-1)/((s+2)(s+3)) are correct?
options: It has a zero in the right half plane
explanation: Both poles are in the LHP so it is stable; the RHP zero makes it non-minimum phase.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 3

topic: Sampling theorem, spectra of sampled signals and aliasing
stem: The Nyquist sampling theorem states that a band-limited signal of maximum frequency fm can be recovered if:
explanation: Sampling at or above twice the highest frequency prevents spectral overlap.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Sampling theorem, spectra of sampled signals and aliasing
stem: The Nyquist rate for a signal band-limited to 4 kHz is:
explanation: Nyquist rate = 2 x fm = 8000 samples per second.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Sampling theorem, spectra of sampled signals and aliasing
stem: The spectrum of an ideally sampled signal consists of:
options: A single copy of the baseband spectrum
Periodic repetitions of the baseband spectrum at multiples of fs
explanation: Multiplication by an impulse train in time convolves the spectrum with an impulse train.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Sampling theorem, spectra of sampled signals and aliasing
stem: Aliasing occurs when:
options: The sampling rate is below twice the highest signal frequency
The sampling rate is very high
explanation: Overlapping spectral replicas make high frequencies masquerade as lower ones.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Sampling theorem, spectra of sampled signals and aliasing
stem: A 6 kHz sinusoid sampled at 8 kHz appears after reconstruction as a tone of:
explanation: The alias appears at |fs - f| = 8 - 6 = 2 kHz.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Sampling theorem, spectra of sampled signals and aliasing
stem: An anti-aliasing filter is placed:
options: Before the sampler, to band-limit the input signal
explanation: Once aliasing occurs it cannot be undone, so filtering must precede sampling.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Sampling theorem, spectra of sampled signals and aliasing
stem: The folding frequency of a sampled system is:
explanation: Frequencies above fs/2 fold back into the baseband as aliases.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Sampling theorem, spectra of sampled signals and aliasing
stem: Natural sampling differs from ideal (impulse) sampling in that:
options: The pulse tops follow the signal, and spectral replicas are weighted by a sinc envelope
explanation: The finite pulse width imposes a sinc-shaped amplitude envelope on the replicas.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Sampling theorem, spectra of sampled signals and aliasing
stem: Bandpass sampling allows a signal of bandwidth B centred at high frequency to be sampled at:
options: Rates as low as 2B under suitable band-positioning conditions
explanation: Deliberate, controlled aliasing places the band in a free spectral slot.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Sampling theorem, spectra of sampled signals and aliasing
stem: Oversampling a signal well above the Nyquist rate is beneficial because it:
options: Relaxes the anti-aliasing filter requirements and spreads quantization noise
explanation: Gentler filter roll-off is allowed and in-band quantization noise is reduced.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Reconstruction: ideal interpolator, zero-order and first-order hold
stem: Ideal reconstruction of a sampled signal requires:
options: An ideal low-pass filter with cut-off fs/2
explanation: It passes the baseband replica and rejects all higher-frequency images.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Reconstruction: ideal interpolator, zero-order and first-order hold
stem: The impulse response of the ideal interpolator is:
explanation: Reconstruction is a sum of sinc functions weighted by the sample values.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Reconstruction: ideal interpolator, zero-order and first-order hold
stem: Ideal reconstruction using sinc interpolation is not physically realizable because:
options: The sinc function is infinite in extent and non-causal
explanation: A practical filter must be causal and of finite length, so an approximation is used.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Reconstruction: ideal interpolator, zero-order and first-order hold
stem: A zero-order hold reconstructs a signal by:
options: Holding each sample constant until the next sample arrives
explanation: Its output is a staircase approximation of the original waveform.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Reconstruction: ideal interpolator, zero-order and first-order hold
stem: The transfer function of a zero-order hold is:
explanation: Its frequency response has a sinc magnitude and a linear phase equal to T/2 delay.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Reconstruction: ideal interpolator, zero-order and first-order hold
stem: The ZOH introduces an effective time delay of approximately:
explanation: This delay erodes phase margin in digital control loops.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Reconstruction: ideal interpolator, zero-order and first-order hold
stem: The sinc-shaped magnitude droop of a ZOH is compensated by:
explanation: The compensator boosts high frequencies to flatten the overall response.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Reconstruction: ideal interpolator, zero-order and first-order hold
stem: A first-order hold reconstructs the signal by:
options: Linear interpolation using the current and previous samples
explanation: It gives a smoother output than a ZOH but adds more delay.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Reconstruction: ideal interpolator, zero-order and first-order hold
stem: Compared with a zero-order hold, a first-order hold generally provides:
options: Better high-frequency accuracy but greater phase lag
explanation: The extra prediction improves the waveform but adds about one sample of delay.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Reconstruction: ideal interpolator, zero-order and first-order hold
stem: The reconstruction (smoothing) filter after a DAC is used to:
options: Remove the spectral images above fs/2 left by the hold circuit
explanation: The ZOH only partially attenuates the images, so an analog low-pass filter follows.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Applications: modulation, filtering and feedback control
stem: Amplitude modulation of a message by a carrier corresponds in the frequency domain to:
options: Shifting the message spectrum to the carrier frequency
explanation: Multiplication in time is convolution in frequency with carrier impulses.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Applications: modulation, filtering and feedback control
stem: The bandwidth of a DSB-SC amplitude modulated signal for a message of bandwidth W is:
explanation: Both upper and lower sidebands are transmitted.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Applications: modulation, filtering and feedback control
stem: Coherent (synchronous) detection of a DSB-SC signal requires:
options: A local carrier matched in frequency and phase
explanation: Phase error causes attenuation, and frequency error causes beating of the recovered signal.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Applications: modulation, filtering and feedback control
stem: An ideal low-pass filter is non-causal because:
options: Its impulse response (a sinc) is non-zero for negative time
explanation: Practical filters approximate the brick-wall response with a finite transition band.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Applications: modulation, filtering and feedback control
stem: Filtering a signal with a linear-phase filter results in:
options: A pure time delay without waveform distortion
explanation: Constant group delay preserves the relative timing of all frequency components.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Applications: modulation, filtering and feedback control
stem: Group delay of a system is defined as:
explanation: Constant group delay means all frequencies are delayed equally.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Applications: modulation, filtering and feedback control
stem: In a feedback control system, the loop gain determines:
explanation: Signal and system theory supplies the frequency-domain tools used to shape it.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Applications: modulation, filtering and feedback control
stem: A matched filter maximises:
options: The output signal-to-noise ratio at the sampling instant
explanation: Its impulse response is the time-reversed conjugate of the expected signal.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Applications: modulation, filtering and feedback control
stem: Pulse code modulation converts an analog signal into a digital one through:
explanation: Quantization is the only irreversible, information-losing step.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Sampling theorem, spectra of sampled signals and aliasing
stem: Sampling a signal at exactly the Nyquist rate is impractical because:
options: An ideal brick-wall filter would be needed for reconstruction
Aliasing is unavoidable at any rate
explanation: Practical systems sample somewhat above the Nyquist rate to allow a guard band.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Sampling theorem, spectra of sampled signals and aliasing
stem: The relation between continuous-time frequency and discrete-time frequency after sampling is:
explanation: The band from -fs/2 to fs/2 maps onto the digital range -pi to pi radians per sample.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Reconstruction: ideal interpolator, zero-order and first-order hold
stem: A practical DAC output before smoothing appears as:
explanation: The internal ZOH holds each code value for one sample period.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Applications: modulation, filtering and feedback control
stem: The autocorrelation function of a signal is related to its power spectral density by:
explanation: PSD is the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation function.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Sampling theorem, spectra of sampled signals and aliasing
stem: Aliasing can be removed by filtering after the signal has been sampled.
explanation: Once spectral overlap occurs the original components are irrecoverably merged.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Reconstruction: ideal interpolator, zero-order and first-order hold
stem: A zero-order hold has a low-pass frequency characteristic.
explanation: Its sinc magnitude response attenuates higher frequencies, partially suppressing images.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Sampling theorem, spectra of sampled signals and aliasing
stem:
Assertion (A): Practical systems sample at a rate higher than the Nyquist rate.
Reason (R): Real signals are never perfectly band-limited and practical filters have finite roll-off.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A guard band between fs/2 and the signal edge accommodates the filter transition region.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Reconstruction: ideal interpolator, zero-order and first-order hold
stem:
Assertion (A): The zero-order hold degrades the stability margin of a digital control loop.
Reason (R): The ZOH introduces an effective delay of about half the sampling period.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: That delay contributes additional phase lag, reducing the available phase margin.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Sampling theorem, spectra of sampled signals and aliasing
stem: Which measures help to avoid aliasing in a data acquisition system?
options: Using an anti-aliasing low-pass filter before the ADC
Using a reconstruction filter after the DAC only
explanation: Aliasing must be prevented before sampling; post-DAC filtering cannot undo it.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 4

topic: Z-transform, region of convergence, poles and zeros
stem: The bilateral Z-transform of x[n] is defined as:
explanation: It is the discrete-time counterpart of the Laplace transform.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-transform, region of convergence, poles and zeros
stem: The Z-transform of the unit impulse delta[n] is:
explanation: Only the n = 0 term survives in the summation.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-transform, region of convergence, poles and zeros
stem: The Z-transform of \(a^n u[n]\) is:
explanation: A right-sided exponential gives a pole at z = a and an ROC outside it.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-transform, region of convergence, poles and zeros
stem: The ROC of a right-sided (causal) sequence is:
options: The exterior of a circle through the outermost pole
explanation: Left-sided sequences give interior ROCs and two-sided sequences give annular ROCs.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-transform, region of convergence, poles and zeros
stem: A discrete LTI system is stable if and only if its ROC:
explanation: Only then does the DTFT exist and h[n] remain absolutely summable.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-transform, region of convergence, poles and zeros
stem: A causal and stable discrete system must have all poles:
explanation: Causality gives an exterior ROC, and stability requires it to include |z| = 1.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-transform, region of convergence, poles and zeros
stem: The ROC of a finite-length sequence is:
options: The entire z-plane except possibly z = 0 or z = infinity
explanation: A finite sum converges everywhere except where negative or positive powers blow up.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-transform, region of convergence, poles and zeros
stem: The time-shifting property of the Z-transform states that x[n - k] transforms to:
explanation: Each unit delay corresponds to multiplication by z^{-1}, the delay operator.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-transform, region of convergence, poles and zeros
stem: Convolution of two sequences corresponds in the z-domain to:
explanation: The ROC of the product contains at least the intersection of the individual ROCs.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-transform, region of convergence, poles and zeros
stem: The Z-transform of \(n a^n u[n]\) is:
explanation: Obtained from the differentiation-in-z property, giving a double pole at z = a.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-transform, region of convergence, poles and zeros
stem: The relation between the Z-transform and the DTFT is:
options: The DTFT is \(X(z)\) evaluated on the unit circle \(z=e^{j\omega}\)
explanation: This requires the ROC to include the unit circle.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-transform, region of convergence, poles and zeros
stem: Two different sequences can have the same algebraic Z-transform expression when:
explanation: The ROC must always be stated to make the inverse transform unique.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-domain analysis and difference equations
stem: The transfer function of a discrete LTI system described by a difference equation is:
options: The ratio of the Z-transform of the output to that of the input with zero initial conditions
explanation: H(z) = Y(z)/X(z) is a rational function of z for LCCDE systems.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-domain analysis and difference equations
stem: For the difference equation \(y[n]-0.5y[n-1]=x[n]\), the transfer function is:
explanation: Transforming both sides gives Y(z)(1 - 0.5z^{-1}) = X(z); the pole is at z = 0.5.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-domain analysis and difference equations
stem: The system y[n] - 2y[n-1] = x[n] with a causal ROC is:
options: Unstable, since the pole at z = 2 lies outside the unit circle
explanation: A causal pole outside the unit circle gives a growing impulse response.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-domain analysis and difference equations
stem: An FIR system is characterised by a transfer function with:
options: Only zeros (poles only at the origin)
explanation: Its impulse response has finite length and it is always stable.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-domain analysis and difference equations
stem: An IIR system differs from an FIR system in that it:
options: Uses feedback of past outputs, giving an infinite-length impulse response
explanation: Recursive terms create poles away from the origin and possible instability.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-domain analysis and difference equations
stem: The unilateral Z-transform is preferred for solving difference equations because:
options: It incorporates initial conditions through the shifting property
explanation: Terms like y[-1] appear explicitly, giving the complete response.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-domain analysis and difference equations
stem: The final value theorem for the Z-transform gives x[infinity] as:
explanation: It is valid only when all poles of (z-1)X(z) are inside the unit circle.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-domain analysis and difference equations
stem: The initial value theorem for a causal sequence states x[0] equals:
explanation: At large z all delayed terms vanish, leaving only the n = 0 term.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-domain analysis and difference equations
stem: Methods available to compute an inverse Z-transform include:
options: Partial fractions, power series (long division) and contour integration
explanation: The choice depends on whether a closed form or numerical samples are needed.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-domain analysis and difference equations
stem: An all-pass discrete system has poles and zeros arranged so that each zero is at:
options: The conjugate reciprocal \(1/a^*\) of a pole at \(a\)
The same location as the pole
explanation: This gives unity magnitude at all frequencies with only phase variation.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-domain analysis and difference equations
stem: A minimum-phase discrete system has:
options: All poles and zeros inside the unit circle
explanation: Such a system has a stable causal inverse.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: System realizations: direct, cascade and parallel forms
stem: Direct Form I realization of an IIR filter uses:
options: Separate delay chains for input and output, requiring more delay elements
explanation: It needs N + M delays, more than Direct Form II.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: System realizations: direct, cascade and parallel forms
stem: Direct Form II is called canonic because it:
options: Uses the minimum possible number of delay elements
explanation: The two delay chains are merged, needing only max(N, M) delays.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: System realizations: direct, cascade and parallel forms
stem: Cascade realization implements H(z) as:
options: A product of first- and second-order sections
explanation: Second-order sections keep conjugate pole pairs together with real coefficients.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: System realizations: direct, cascade and parallel forms
stem: Parallel realization implements the transfer function as:
options: A sum of first- and second-order sections from a partial fraction expansion
explanation: Each section's output is summed, and errors do not propagate between sections.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: System realizations: direct, cascade and parallel forms
stem: Cascade and parallel forms are preferred over the direct form for high-order filters because:
options: They are far less sensitive to coefficient quantization errors
explanation: Grouping poles into low-order sections limits the movement of pole locations.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: System realizations: direct, cascade and parallel forms
stem: The number of delay elements in a canonic realization of an Nth order IIR filter is:
explanation: Direct Form II shares one delay chain between the recursive and non-recursive parts.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: System realizations: direct, cascade and parallel forms
stem: A transposed Direct Form II structure is obtained by:
options: Reversing all signal flow directions and interchanging input and output
explanation: Transposition preserves the transfer function but can improve numerical behaviour.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: System realizations: direct, cascade and parallel forms
stem: Lattice structures are attractive for digital filters because they:
options: Have low sensitivity to coefficient quantization and give a simple stability check
explanation: Stability is guaranteed if all reflection coefficients have magnitude less than one.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: System realizations: direct, cascade and parallel forms
stem: A signal flow graph representation of a digital filter shows:
options: Adders, multipliers and unit delay elements and their interconnections
explanation: It maps directly onto the hardware or software implementation.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: System realizations: direct, cascade and parallel forms
stem: For a linear-phase FIR filter, the impulse response coefficients must be:
options: Symmetric or antisymmetric about the centre
explanation: Coefficient symmetry also halves the number of required multiplications.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-transform, region of convergence, poles and zeros
stem: The region of convergence of a Z-transform can contain poles.
explanation: The transform diverges at a pole, so poles are always excluded from the ROC.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: System realizations: direct, cascade and parallel forms
stem: An FIR filter is always stable regardless of its coefficients.
explanation: Its impulse response has finite length, so it is always absolutely summable.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: System realizations: direct, cascade and parallel forms
stem:
Assertion (A): Cascade and parallel realizations are preferred for high-order digital filters.
Reason (R): Direct-form structures are highly sensitive to coefficient quantization at high orders.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Breaking the filter into low-order sections limits pole displacement due to finite wordlength.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-transform, region of convergence, poles and zeros
stem:
Assertion (A): A causal system with all poles inside the unit circle is stable.
Reason (R): Causality makes the ROC the exterior of the outermost pole, which then includes the unit circle.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The ROC containing |z| = 1 is precisely the condition for BIBO stability.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Z-domain analysis and difference equations
stem: Which statements about FIR filters compared with IIR filters are correct?
options: FIR filters can have exactly linear phase
FIR filters generally need a higher order for the same magnitude specification
explanation: FIR filters are non-recursive; the absence of feedback gives stability and linear phase at the cost of order.
source: BEU syllabus — Signals and Systems, Unit 5

topic: Concentrated winding
stem: A concentrated winding is one in which all the conductors of a coil group are:
options: Placed in a single pair of slots
explanation: A distributed winding spreads the conductors over several slots per pole per phase, giving a better MMF wave.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Distributed winding
stem: AC machine windings are distributed over several slots mainly to:
options: Obtain a nearly sinusoidal MMF and e.m.f. waveform with better copper utilisation
explanation: Distribution suppresses harmonics and improves heat dissipation, at the cost of a slightly reduced fundamental.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Winding distribution factor
stem: The distribution (breadth) factor of an AC winding is given by:
explanation: Here m is slots per pole per phase and β the slot angle; k_d is always slightly less than unity.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Winding distribution factor
stem: A three-phase, 4-pole alternator has 36 slots. The slot angle and slots per pole per phase are:
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Winding distribution factor
stem: The pitch (coil span) factor of a winding with a coil span short of full pitch by an angle \(\alpha\) is:
explanation: Short pitching slightly reduces the fundamental but strongly suppresses selected harmonics.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Air-gap MMF distribution with fixed current through winding-concentrated and distributed
stem: The air-gap MMF produced by a concentrated full-pitch coil carrying DC is:
explanation: Distributing the winding over several slots makes the MMF a stepped wave approaching a sinusoid.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Pulsating magnetic field - alternating current in windings with spatial displacement
stem: A single winding carrying alternating current produces a magnetic field that is:
options: Pulsating, fixed in space but varying sinusoidally in magnitude
explanation: A pulsating field can be resolved into two counter-rotating fields of half amplitude.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Three windings spatially shifted by 120 degrees (carrying three-phase balanced currents)
stem: Three windings displaced 120° in space and carrying balanced three-phase currents produce:
options: A revolving field of constant magnitude 1.5 times the peak MMF of one phase
explanation: The three pulsating MMFs combine into a rotating wave travelling at synchronous speed.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Revolving magnetic field
stem: The speed of the revolving magnetic field in an AC machine is:
explanation: Synchronous speed in r.p.m. depends only on the supply frequency and the number of poles.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Revolving magnetic field
stem: A 6-pole, 50 Hz three-phase induction motor has a synchronous speed of:
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Construction
stem: The stator core of an induction motor is laminated in order to:
explanation: Insulated laminations break up the eddy current paths, since the loss varies as the square of thickness.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Types (squirrel cage and slip-ring)
stem: The essential advantage of a slip-ring induction motor over a squirrel cage motor is that it:
options: Permits external rotor resistance for high starting torque and speed control
explanation: Cage rotors are rugged and cheap but their rotor resistance is fixed and inaccessible.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Torque Slip Characteristics
stem: The slip of an induction motor is defined as:
explanation: Typical full-load slip is 2–5%; at standstill the slip is unity.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Torque Slip Characteristics
stem: A 4-pole, 50 Hz induction motor runs at 1455 r.p.m. Its slip is:
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Torque Slip Characteristics
stem: The frequency of the rotor current in an induction motor with slip s is:
explanation: At 4% slip on a 50 Hz supply, the rotor frequency is only 2 Hz.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Torque Slip Characteristics
stem: In an induction motor, the ratio of rotor copper loss to rotor input power equals:
explanation: Rotor input divides as sP₂ in copper loss and (1−s)P₂ as mechanical power, so efficiency falls with slip.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Starting and Maximum Torque. Equivalent circuit. Phasor Diagram
stem: Maximum torque in an induction motor occurs at a slip given by:
explanation: Maximum torque occurs when the rotor resistance per unit slip equals the standstill rotor reactance.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Starting and Maximum Torque. Equivalent circuit. Phasor Diagram
stem: The maximum torque of an induction motor is:
options: Inversely proportional to the square of voltage
Independent of rotor resistance, though the slip at which it occurs is not
explanation: Adding rotor resistance shifts the peak toward higher slip without changing its magnitude.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Starting and Maximum Torque. Equivalent circuit. Phasor Diagram
stem: The torque of an induction motor varies with the applied stator voltage as:
explanation: A 10% voltage dip therefore reduces the torque by about 19%, which is critical during starting.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Effect of parameter variation on torque speed characteristics (variation of rotor and stator resistances
stem: Adding external resistance to the rotor circuit of a slip-ring induction motor:
options: Increases the starting torque and the slip at maximum torque
explanation: Maximum torque can be made to occur at standstill when the added resistance equals the rotor reactance.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Methods of starting
stem: A star-delta starter reduces the starting current of an induction motor to:
explanation: Star connection applies 1/√3 of the voltage, so both line current and starting torque fall to one-third.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Methods of starting
stem: With an autotransformer starter using a tapping ratio x, the starting torque is reduced to:
explanation: Torque varies as the square of the applied voltage, and the line current also falls as x².
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Methods of starting
stem: Direct-on-line starting of an induction motor draws a starting current of about:
explanation: This heavy inrush causes voltage dips, so DOL is limited to small motors.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Braking and speed control for induction motors. Generator operation. Self-excitation. Doubly-Fed Induction Machine
stem: The most efficient and widely used method of speed control of a cage induction motor is:
options: Variable frequency control maintaining constant V/f
explanation: Constant V/f keeps the air-gap flux constant, giving full torque over a wide speed range.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Braking and speed control for induction motors. Generator operation. Self-excitation. Doubly-Fed Induction Machine
stem: An induction machine operates as a generator when its slip is:
options: Negative, that is the rotor is driven above synchronous speed
explanation: Above synchronous speed the torque reverses and the machine feeds power back into the supply.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Braking and speed control for induction motors. Generator operation. Self-excitation. Doubly-Fed Induction Machine
stem: Plugging of an induction motor is achieved by:
options: Interchanging two supply leads so that the slip becomes greater than unity
explanation: Reversing the field direction produces a large braking torque, but the rotor heating is severe.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Braking and speed control for induction motors. Generator operation. Self-excitation. Doubly-Fed Induction Machine
stem: A doubly-fed induction generator (DFIG) is widely used in wind energy because it:
options: Allows variable speed operation with a converter rated for only a fraction of the machine rating
explanation: Only the slip power passes through the rotor-side converter, typically about 30% of rated power.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Losses and Efficiency
stem: In an induction motor, the no-load test gives:
options: Core loss, friction and windage loss, and the magnetising branch parameters
explanation: The blocked-rotor test correspondingly gives the equivalent series impedance and copper losses.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Losses and Efficiency
stem: If the rotor input of an induction motor is 10 kW at a slip of 4%, the rotor copper loss is:
explanation: Rotor copper loss = sP₂ = 0.04 × 10 000 = 400 W, leaving 9.6 kW as mechanical power.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Losses and Efficiency
stem: The maximum possible efficiency of the rotor of an induction motor equals:
explanation: Mechanical power is (1−s) times the rotor input, so low slip is essential for high efficiency.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Torque Slip Characteristics
stem: On the torque-slip curve, the stable operating region of an induction motor lies:
options: Between zero slip and the slip at maximum torque
explanation: In this region an increase in load slows the rotor and raises the torque, restoring equilibrium.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Construction
stem: The air gap of an induction motor is kept as small as mechanically possible in order to:
options: Minimise the magnetising current and improve the power factor
explanation: A large gap needs more MMF for the same flux, worsening the already lagging power factor.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Types (squirrel cage and slip-ring)
stem: Rotor slots of a squirrel cage induction motor are usually skewed to:
explanation: Skewing also reduces harmonic torques that can cause crawling at sub-synchronous speeds.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Revolving magnetic field
stem: An induction motor can never run at synchronous speed under load.
explanation: Without relative motion no rotor e.m.f. is induced, so no torque could be developed.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Methods of starting
stem: A star-delta starter reduces the starting torque to one-third of the direct-on-line value.
explanation: Phase voltage falls by √3, so torque, being proportional to V², falls to one-third.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Three windings spatially shifted by 120 degrees (carrying three-phase balanced currents)
stem:
Assertion (A): A three-phase induction motor is self-starting.
Reason (R): Balanced three-phase currents in windings displaced 120° produce a revolving magnetic field.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The rotating field induces rotor currents that produce starting torque, exactly as R explains.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Starting and Maximum Torque. Equivalent circuit. Phasor Diagram
stem:
Assertion (A): External rotor resistance is used to obtain high starting torque in slip-ring motors.
Reason (R): Maximum torque occurs at a slip equal to \(R_2/X_2\), so increasing \(R_2\) moves the peak toward standstill.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Making R₂ equal to X₂ places maximum torque at s = 1, precisely the mechanism R describes.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Torque Slip Characteristics
stem: Which statements about a three-phase induction motor are correct? (Select all that apply)
options: Rotor copper loss equals s times the rotor input
Torque is proportional to the square of the applied voltage
Maximum torque is proportional to rotor resistance
explanation: Maximum torque is independent of rotor resistance; only the slip at which it occurs depends on R₂.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 1

topic: Single-phase induction motor: Constructional features
stem: A single-phase induction motor with only a main winding is:
options: Not self-starting, though it runs once given an initial rotation
explanation: A single winding produces a pulsating field with zero net starting torque, so an auxiliary phase is needed.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Double revolving field theory
stem: According to double revolving field theory, the pulsating field of a single-phase motor is resolved into:
options: Two fields of half amplitude revolving in opposite directions
explanation: At standstill the two fields give equal and opposite torques, so the net starting torque is zero.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Double revolving field theory
stem: Once a single-phase induction motor is running at slip s with respect to the forward field, its slip with respect to the backward field is:
explanation: The backward field rotates oppositely, so the relative slip is nearly 2 at normal running speed.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Determination of parameters. Split-phase starting methods and applications; Universal Series Motor
stem: In a capacitor-start single-phase induction motor, the capacitor is connected in series with the:
explanation: The capacitor gives the auxiliary current a phase lead, producing an approximately rotating field at start.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Determination of parameters. Split-phase starting methods and applications; Universal Series Motor
stem: The centrifugal switch in a split-phase motor serves to:
options: Disconnect the starting winding at about 75% of synchronous speed
explanation: The high-resistance auxiliary winding would overheat if left permanently in circuit.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Determination of parameters. Split-phase starting methods and applications; Universal Series Motor
stem: A shaded-pole motor is generally used for applications requiring:
options: Very low starting torque and small power, such as fans
explanation: It is the simplest and cheapest single-phase motor but has poor efficiency and low starting torque.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Determination of parameters. Split-phase starting methods and applications; Universal Series Motor
stem: A universal motor can operate on both AC and DC supplies because it is essentially a:
options: Series-wound motor in which torque direction is unchanged when both flux and current reverse
explanation: Simultaneous reversal of field and armature current keeps the torque unidirectional.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Determination of parameters. Split-phase starting methods and applications; Universal Series Motor
stem: Universal motors are widely used in mixers and drills because they offer:
options: High speed and high starting torque with a small size
explanation: Series characteristics give large torque at low speed, though brushes require periodic maintenance.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Constructional features
stem: In a conventional synchronous machine, the field winding is placed on the:
explanation: A stationary armature simplifies insulation of the high-voltage AC winding and current collection.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Constructional features
stem: Salient pole rotors are generally used for:
options: Low-speed hydro generators with many poles
explanation: Cylindrical (non-salient) rotors suit 3000 r.p.m. steam turbines because of their mechanical strength.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Cylindrical rotor synchronous machine - generated EMF
stem: The e.m.f. equation of an alternator is:
explanation: The pitch and distribution factors account for the winding not being fully concentrated and full pitched.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Cylindrical rotor synchronous machine - generated EMF
stem: The frequency of the e.m.f. generated by an alternator running at N r.p.m. with P poles is:
explanation: A 4-pole machine must run at 1500 r.p.m. to generate 50 Hz.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Armature reaction
stem: The armature reaction of an alternator supplying a purely inductive (zero p.f. lagging) load is:
explanation: At zero p.f. leading it is wholly magnetising, and at unity p.f. purely cross-magnetising.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Armature reaction
stem: At unity power factor, the armature reaction of an alternator is:
explanation: The armature MMF acts at right angles to the main field, distorting but not weakening it overall.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Synchronous impedance
stem: The synchronous impedance of an alternator is:
options: \(Z_s=R_a+jX_s\), where \(X_s\) includes leakage and armature reaction reactance
explanation: Armature reaction is represented as a fictitious reactance added to the leakage reactance.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Synchronous impedance
stem: The synchronous impedance method of finding voltage regulation is called the pessimistic method because it:
options: Cannot be used for salient pole machines
Gives a value of regulation higher than the actual
explanation: Assuming an unsaturated magnetic circuit overestimates the synchronous reactance and hence the voltage drop.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Voltage regulation
stem: The voltage regulation of an alternator is negative when the load power factor is:
explanation: A leading load causes a magnetising armature reaction that raises the terminal voltage above no-load value.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Voltage regulation
stem: The zero power factor (Potier) method of determining regulation separates:
options: Leakage reactance from armature reaction MMF
explanation: The Potier triangle gives the leakage reactance, so the method is more accurate than the EMF method.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Operating characteristics of synchronous machines
stem: A synchronous motor running on no load with over-excitation behaves as a:
explanation: Over-excited synchronous machines supply reactive power, so they are used for power factor correction.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: V-curves. Salient pole machine - two reaction theory
stem: The V-curve of a synchronous motor is a plot of:
options: Armature current against field current at constant load
explanation: Armature current is minimum at unity power factor, rising on either side, giving the characteristic V shape.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: V-curves. Salient pole machine - two reaction theory
stem: In Blondel's two-reaction theory for salient pole machines, the armature MMF is resolved along the:
explanation: Non-uniform air gap gives different reactances along the pole axis and the interpolar axis.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Power angle characteristics
stem: The power developed by a cylindrical rotor synchronous machine varies with the load angle \(\delta\) as:
explanation: Maximum (pull-out) power occurs at δ = 90°, beyond which the machine loses synchronism.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Power angle characteristics
stem: The steady-state stability limit of a cylindrical rotor synchronous machine occurs at a load angle of:
explanation: Beyond 90° the slope dP/dδ becomes negative, so any disturbance causes loss of synchronism.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Power angle characteristics
stem: A salient pole machine develops, in addition to the excitation power, a:
explanation: The difference between X_d and X_q gives reluctance torque, which peaks at δ = 45°.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Parallel operation of alternators - synchronization and load division; starting and speed control of synchronous motor
stem: Which of the following is NOT a necessary condition for synchronising an alternator to the bus?
options: Equal kVA ratings of the machines
explanation: Voltage, frequency, phase sequence and phase angle must match, but the ratings need not be equal.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Parallel operation of alternators - synchronization and load division; starting and speed control of synchronous motor
stem: After an alternator is synchronised to an infinite bus, increasing its excitation alone will:
options: Increase the reactive power delivered without changing the active power
explanation: Active power is controlled by the prime mover input, while excitation governs the reactive power.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Parallel operation of alternators - synchronization and load division; starting and speed control of synchronous motor
stem: A synchronous motor is not self-starting because:
options: The rotor cannot follow the rapidly revolving stator field from standstill
explanation: Damper (amortisseur) bars start it as an induction motor before the DC field is applied.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Parallel operation of alternators - synchronization and load division; starting and speed control of synchronous motor
stem: Hunting in a synchronous machine refers to:
options: Oscillation of the rotor about its equilibrium load angle after a disturbance
explanation: Damper windings suppress hunting by inducing currents that oppose the relative oscillatory motion.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Reluctance Machines: Synchronous reluctance
stem: A synchronous reluctance motor develops torque because of:
options: A DC field winding on the rotor
The tendency of the rotor to align along the minimum reluctance path
explanation: Rotor saliency creates a difference between X_d and X_q, producing reluctance torque with no rotor excitation.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Stepper motors
stem: A stepper motor is best described as a device that:
options: Runs only at synchronous speed continuously
Converts digital pulses into discrete angular movements
explanation: Each input pulse advances the shaft by one fixed step angle, giving open-loop position control.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Stepper motors
stem: A stepper motor with a step angle of 1.8° requires how many pulses for one complete revolution?
explanation: 360/1.8 = 200 steps per revolution, typical of a hybrid stepper motor.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: And switched reluctance machines
stem: A switched reluctance motor requires:
options: Electronic commutation with rotor position sensing
explanation: Its doubly salient structure has no rotor winding or magnets, so phases must be energised in sequence.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Steady-state and dynamic performance of PM synchronous machines
stem: A permanent magnet synchronous motor has the advantage of:
options: No field copper loss, giving higher efficiency and power density
explanation: Eliminating rotor excitation removes the associated I²R loss, though the flux can no longer be varied freely.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: And Brushless DC machines
stem: In a brushless DC motor, commutation is performed by:
options: Electronic switches controlled by rotor position sensors
explanation: Hall sensors or sensorless back-EMF detection sequence the inverter, eliminating brush wear.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Servo Motors: Working principle and applications
stem: A servo motor used in control systems is characterised by:
options: Low inertia and a linear torque-speed characteristic for rapid response
explanation: A long narrow rotor minimises inertia, giving the fast acceleration required for position control.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Double revolving field theory
stem: A single-phase induction motor produces zero starting torque with only its main winding energised.
explanation: Forward and backward revolving fields give equal and opposite torques at standstill.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Operating characteristics of synchronous machines
stem: A synchronous motor runs at constant speed irrespective of load, until it pulls out of synchronism.
explanation: The rotor locks to the revolving field at N_s = 120f/P; only the load angle changes with load.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Operating characteristics of synchronous machines
stem:
Assertion (A): An over-excited synchronous motor is used to improve the power factor of an industrial plant.
Reason (R): When over-excited it draws a leading current, supplying reactive power to the system.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Leading VARs offset the lagging VARs of induction motors, which is the synchronous condenser action R describes.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Power angle characteristics
stem:
Assertion (A): A synchronous generator loses synchronism if the load angle exceeds 90°.
Reason (R): Beyond 90° the synchronising power coefficient \(dP/d\delta\) becomes negative.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A negative slope means a disturbance is amplified rather than corrected, so R correctly explains A.
source: BEU syllabus — Electrical Machine-II, Unit 2

topic: Constructional features
stem: Which statements about synchronous machines are correct? (Select all that apply)
options: The field winding is on the rotor and carries DC
An over-excited machine supplies reactive power
A synchronous motor is inherently self-starting
explanation: Synchronous motors need damper bars or an auxiliary drive to start, so the last statement is false.
