explanation: Beyond this the output waveform becomes badly distorted.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Cyclo-converter classification, step up and step down
stem: The main industrial application of cyclo-converters is:
options: Very large low speed AC motor drives such as ball mills and ship propulsion
explanation: They handle multi-megawatt ratings with rugged line commutated thyristors.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Cyclo-converter classification, step up and step down
stem: Compared with a DC link converter, a cyclo-converter has the advantage of:
options: No intermediate energy storage element and inherent four quadrant operation
explanation: Its drawbacks are poor input power factor and a large device count.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Cyclo-converter classification, step up and step down
stem: The input power factor of a cyclo-converter is:
options: Poor and lagging, worsening as the output voltage is reduced
explanation: Large firing angles at low output voltage draw substantial reactive power.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Cyclo-converter classification, step up and step down
stem: A matrix converter differs from a cyclo-converter in that it:
options: Uses bidirectional force commutated switches and can produce output above the supply frequency
explanation: Its output voltage is limited to 0.866 of the input magnitude.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Single phase to single phase and three phase to single phase cyclo-converters
stem: A single-phase to single-phase cyclo-converter consists of:
options: Two full converters (positive and negative groups) connected in anti-parallel
explanation: The positive group produces the positive half of the output and the negative group the other half.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Single phase to single phase and three phase to single phase cyclo-converters
stem: In a single-phase cyclo-converter with a resistive load:
options: The load current is in phase with the voltage, so each group conducts for a complete half cycle
explanation: The group changeover instant coincides with the voltage zero crossing.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Single phase to single phase and three phase to single phase cyclo-converters
stem: With an RL load, the output current of a cyclo-converter lags the voltage, so:
options: Each converter group operates in both rectifier and inverter modes during a cycle
explanation: Energy is returned to the supply during the inverting intervals.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Single phase to single phase and three phase to single phase cyclo-converters
stem: In circulating current free (blocking) mode operation:
options: Only one converter group is gated at a time and a dead time is provided at changeover
explanation: A zero current detector must confirm extinction before enabling the other group.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Single phase to single phase and three phase to single phase cyclo-converters
stem: In circulating current mode operation, an inter-group reactor is used to:
options: Limit the circulating current between the two simultaneously gated groups
explanation: This mode gives a better output waveform and continuous conduction at all loads.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Single phase to single phase and three phase to single phase cyclo-converters
stem: For circulating current operation the firing angles of the two groups must satisfy:
explanation: This makes the mean output voltages of the two groups equal and opposing.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Single phase to single phase and three phase to single phase cyclo-converters
stem: A three-phase to single-phase cyclo-converter typically uses:
options: Two three-phase bridge converters in anti-parallel, needing 12 thyristors
explanation: Its output waveform is much smoother than the single-phase version.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Single phase to single phase and three phase to single phase cyclo-converters
stem: A three-phase half wave (three pulse) cyclo-converter group uses how many thyristors per group?
explanation: A dual three pulse cyclo-converter therefore needs six thyristors in total.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Single phase to single phase and three phase to single phase cyclo-converters
stem: Increasing the pulse number of a cyclo-converter improves:
options: The maximum output frequency to infinity
The output waveform quality and reduces harmonic content
The input power factor to unity
explanation: Twelve pulse arrangements are common in large drive installations.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Cosine wave crossing control, three phase to three phase and output voltage equation
stem: The cosine wave crossing technique determines the firing angle by:
options: Comparing a cosine timing wave synchronised to the supply with the reference signal
explanation: The intersection instant gives alpha = arccos(Vr/Vm).
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Cosine wave crossing control, three phase to three phase and output voltage equation
stem: The main advantage of cosine wave crossing control is that:
options: The average output voltage becomes linearly proportional to the reference signal
explanation: The arccos characteristic exactly cancels the cosine dependence of the converter.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Cosine wave crossing control, three phase to three phase and output voltage equation
stem: In cosine wave crossing control, the firing angle for a reference of zero volts is:
explanation: cos 90 = 0, giving zero average output voltage.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Cosine wave crossing control, three phase to three phase and output voltage equation
stem: If the cosine timing wave has peak Vm and the reference is Vr, the firing angle is:
explanation: The cosine wave must lead the supply phase voltage by 90 degrees.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Cosine wave crossing control, three phase to three phase and output voltage equation
stem: For a cyclo-converter the average output voltage per segment varies as:
explanation: Vdo is the maximum average output at zero firing angle.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Cosine wave crossing control, three phase to three phase and output voltage equation
stem: The fundamental RMS output voltage of a cyclo-converter is given by:
options: \(V_{o1}=rV_{do}/\sqrt2\) where r is the voltage ratio
explanation: The output voltage ratio r must be less than or equal to unity.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Cosine wave crossing control, three phase to three phase and output voltage equation
stem: The firing angle in a cyclo-converter is modulated sinusoidally so that:
options: The mean output voltage traces a sine wave at the desired output frequency
explanation: alpha varies as arccos(r sin(wo t)) over the output cycle.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Cosine wave crossing control, three phase to three phase and output voltage equation
stem: A three-phase to three-phase cyclo-converter using six pulse bridges requires:
explanation: Three output phases each need a dual bridge of 12 devices.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Cosine wave crossing control, three phase to three phase and output voltage equation
stem: A three-phase to three-phase cyclo-converter built from three pulse groups needs:
explanation: Each output phase uses a dual three pulse group of six devices.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Cosine wave crossing control, three phase to three phase and output voltage equation
stem: The output voltage harmonics of a cyclo-converter are:
options: Sub-harmonic and inter-harmonic components related to both input and output frequencies
Only odd multiples of the output frequency
explanation: These beat frequencies make output filtering difficult.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Cosine wave crossing control, three phase to three phase and output voltage equation
stem: For a three-phase output cyclo-converter, the reference signals for the three phases are:
options: Displaced by 120 degrees at the desired output frequency
explanation: The same cosine crossing hardware serves each phase independently.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Cyclo-converter classification, step up and step down
stem: An AC voltage controller differs from a cyclo-converter in that it:
options: Changes only the output voltage magnitude, keeping the frequency the same
explanation: It uses phase angle control or integral cycle control of back to back thyristors.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Cyclo-converter classification, step up and step down
stem: A step down cyclo-converter can use natural line commutation.
explanation: The supply voltage reversal turns off the conducting thyristors.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Cosine wave crossing control, three phase to three phase and output voltage equation
stem: In cosine wave crossing control the output voltage is a nonlinear function of the reference.
explanation: The arccos firing law makes the average output directly proportional to the reference.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Single phase to single phase and three phase to single phase cyclo-converters
stem:
Assertion (A): Blocking mode cyclo-converters require a dead time at group changeover.
Reason (R): Gating both groups while load current is still flowing would cause a supply short circuit.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A zero current detector confirms extinction before the other group is enabled.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Cyclo-converter classification, step up and step down
stem:
Assertion (A): Cyclo-converters are limited to low output frequencies.
Reason (R): Natural commutation requires several supply half cycles to synthesise each output half cycle.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: In practice the output is kept below about one third of the supply frequency.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Cyclo-converter classification, step up and step down
stem: Which are characteristics of a step down cyclo-converter?
options: Direct AC to AC conversion without a DC link
Output frequency higher than the supply
explanation: By definition a step down cyclo-converter produces an output frequency below the supply frequency.
source: BEU syllabus — Power Electronics, Unit 7

topic: Principles of Amplitude Modulation
stem: Modulation is necessary in a communication system mainly to:
options: Reduce antenna size and allow frequency division multiplexing
explanation: Antenna length must be comparable to a quarter of the wavelength.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: Principles of Amplitude Modulation
stem: In amplitude modulation, the parameter of the carrier that varies is its:
options: Amplitude, in proportion to the message signal
explanation: The carrier frequency and phase remain unchanged.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: Principles of Amplitude Modulation
stem: The modulation index of an AM wave is given by:
explanation: Values above unity cause over-modulation and envelope distortion.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: Principles of Amplitude Modulation
stem: An AM wave has Vmax = 15 V and Vmin = 5 V. Its modulation index is:
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: Principles of Amplitude Modulation
stem: The bandwidth of a conventional AM signal with a message of maximum frequency fm is:
explanation: Upper and lower sidebands each extend fm from the carrier.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: Principles of Amplitude Modulation
stem: The total power of an AM wave with modulation index mu is:
explanation: Pc is the unmodulated carrier power.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: Principles of Amplitude Modulation
stem: For 100% modulation, the fraction of total AM power in the sidebands is:
explanation: Ps/Pt = 0.5/1.5 = 33.3%, so AM is power inefficient.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: Principles of Amplitude Modulation
stem: Over-modulation of an AM signal (mu greater than 1) results in:
options: Envelope distortion and the generation of spurious sidebands
explanation: A simple envelope detector cannot recover the message correctly.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: Principles of Amplitude Modulation
stem: A square law modulator generates AM by:
options: Passing the sum of carrier and message through a nonlinear device and band-pass filtering
explanation: The squared term produces the required product component.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: Principles of Amplitude Modulation
stem: An AM transmitter with 1 kW carrier power modulated to 50% radiates a total power of:
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: DSBSC, SSB-SC and VSB-SC
stem: In DSB-SC modulation:
options: The carrier is suppressed and only the two sidebands are transmitted
explanation: All the transmitted power then carries information.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: DSBSC, SSB-SC and VSB-SC
stem: The bandwidth of a DSB-SC signal compared with conventional AM is:
explanation: Only the carrier component is removed, not a sideband.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: DSBSC, SSB-SC and VSB-SC
stem: A DSB-SC signal is generated using:
options: A balanced modulator or ring modulator
explanation: Balanced operation cancels the carrier at the output.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: DSBSC, SSB-SC and VSB-SC
stem: Demodulation of a DSB-SC signal requires:
options: Coherent (synchronous) detection with a locally generated carrier
explanation: A phase or frequency error in the local carrier distorts the output.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: DSBSC, SSB-SC and VSB-SC
stem: The bandwidth of an SSB-SC signal is:
explanation: Halving the bandwidth allows twice as many channels in a band.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: DSBSC, SSB-SC and VSB-SC
stem: SSB generation by the filter method requires:
options: A sharp cut-off band-pass filter after a balanced modulator
explanation: Filtering is difficult when the message has significant low frequency content.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: DSBSC, SSB-SC and VSB-SC
stem: The phase shift method of SSB generation uses:
options: Two balanced modulators and two 90 degree phase shifters
explanation: Adding or subtracting the outputs selects the lower or upper sideband.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: DSBSC, SSB-SC and VSB-SC
stem: Vestigial sideband modulation is used in television video transmission because:
options: The video signal has significant low frequency content that SSB filters cannot handle
explanation: A vestige of the unwanted sideband is retained for easier filtering.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: DSBSC, SSB-SC and VSB-SC
stem: Compared with conventional AM, SSB-SC offers a power saving because:
options: Both the carrier and one redundant sideband are eliminated
explanation: Its drawback is the need for complex synchronous detection.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: DSBSC, SSB-SC and VSB-SC
stem: A Costas loop is used in DSB-SC reception to:
options: Recover the carrier phase for synchronous demodulation
explanation: It uses in-phase and quadrature arms to derive a phase error signal.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: AM Transmitters and Receivers
stem: A high level AM transmitter performs modulation at:
explanation: Low level modulation instead requires linear amplifiers afterwards.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: AM Transmitters and Receivers
stem: The superheterodyne receiver converts every incoming station to:
options: A fixed intermediate frequency for uniform selectivity and gain
explanation: The standard AM broadcast IF is 455 kHz.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: AM Transmitters and Receivers
stem: The image frequency in a superheterodyne receiver is separated from the desired signal by:
explanation: RF selectivity ahead of the mixer suppresses it.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: AM Transmitters and Receivers
stem: An envelope detector can be used for conventional AM because:
options: The envelope of the modulated wave follows the message when mu is less than 1
explanation: It is a simple diode, resistor and capacitor circuit.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: AM Transmitters and Receivers
stem: Diagonal clipping in an envelope detector occurs when:
options: The RC time constant is too large to follow rapid envelope changes
explanation: The condition RC less than 1/(2 pi fm) times a factor avoids it.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: AM Transmitters and Receivers
stem: Automatic gain control in a receiver is used to:
options: Keep the output level nearly constant despite varying signal strength
explanation: A DC voltage derived from the detector biases the IF amplifiers.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: AM Transmitters and Receivers
stem: Selectivity of a receiver refers to its ability to:
options: Reject adjacent channel signals while accepting the wanted one
explanation: Sensitivity, by contrast, is the ability to receive weak signals.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: AM Transmitters and Receivers
stem: The local oscillator of an AM superheterodyne receiver normally operates:
options: Above the incoming signal frequency by the IF
explanation: High side injection needs a smaller oscillator tuning ratio.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: AM Transmitters and Receivers
stem: Double spotting in a receiver is caused by:
options: Poor front end selectivity allowing a station to be received at two dial settings
explanation: It is a symptom of inadequate image rejection.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: AM Transmitters and Receivers
stem: The noise figure of a receiver is defined as:
options: The ratio of input SNR to output SNR
explanation: The first stage dominates the overall noise figure, per the Friis formula.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: DSBSC, SSB-SC and VSB-SC
stem: SSB-SC transmission requires half the bandwidth of conventional AM.
explanation: Only one sideband of width fm is transmitted instead of two.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: Principles of Amplitude Modulation
stem: In 100% AM modulation, most of the transmitted power lies in the sidebands.
explanation: Two thirds of the power stays in the carrier, which conveys no information.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: DSBSC, SSB-SC and VSB-SC
stem:
Assertion (A): DSB-SC is more power efficient than conventional AM.
Reason (R): Suppressing the carrier removes the component that carries no information.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: All transmitted power then goes into the information bearing sidebands.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: AM Transmitters and Receivers
stem:
Assertion (A): The superheterodyne receiver gives uniform selectivity across the tuning band.
Reason (R): Every received station is translated to the same fixed intermediate frequency.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The IF amplifier filters can therefore be optimised once for all channels.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: DSBSC, SSB-SC and VSB-SC
stem: Which modulation schemes require coherent detection at the receiver?
options: Conventional AM with mu less than 1
explanation: Conventional AM retains the carrier so a simple envelope detector suffices.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 1

topic: Frequency and Phase Modulation
stem: In frequency modulation, the instantaneous carrier frequency varies:
options: In proportion to the amplitude of the modulating signal
explanation: The carrier amplitude stays constant throughout.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Frequency and Phase Modulation
stem: In phase modulation, the instantaneous phase deviation is proportional to:
explanation: FM is equivalent to PM of the integrated message signal.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Frequency and Phase Modulation
stem: The modulation index of an FM signal is:
explanation: Delta f is the peak frequency deviation.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Frequency and Phase Modulation
stem: An FM signal has a peak deviation of 75 kHz and a modulating frequency of 15 kHz. Its modulation index is:
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Frequency and Phase Modulation
stem: Unlike AM, the total transmitted power of an FM signal:
options: Remains constant regardless of the modulation index
explanation: Modulation only redistributes power among the sidebands.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Frequency and Phase Modulation
stem: Narrowband FM is characterised by a modulation index:
options: Much less than 1, giving a spectrum similar to AM
explanation: Its bandwidth is approximately 2fm, like AM.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Frequency and Phase Modulation
stem: The sidebands of an FM signal have amplitudes given by:
options: Bessel functions of the first kind of order n and argument beta
explanation: Theoretically an infinite number of sidebands exists.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Frequency and Phase Modulation
stem: For certain values of the FM modulation index such as 2.405, the carrier component:
options: Vanishes completely, because J0(beta) becomes zero
explanation: This effect is used to calibrate frequency deviation meters.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Frequency and Phase Modulation
stem: For a given modulating amplitude, doubling the modulating frequency in FM:
options: Halves the modulation index while the deviation stays the same
explanation: In PM, by contrast, the deviation is proportional to the message frequency.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Frequency and Phase Modulation
stem: FM is preferred over AM for high fidelity broadcasting because it:
options: Offers superior noise immunity through amplitude limiting
explanation: Noise principally affects amplitude, which the limiter removes.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Transmission bandwidth of FM signals
stem: Carson's rule gives the FM transmission bandwidth as:
explanation: It captures about 98% of the total signal power.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Transmission bandwidth of FM signals
stem: Using Carson's rule for a deviation of 75 kHz and fm of 15 kHz, the bandwidth is:
explanation: B = 2(75 + 15) = 180 kHz, close to the 200 kHz channel allocation.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Transmission bandwidth of FM signals
stem: Commercial FM broadcast in India and most countries uses a channel spacing of:
options: 200 kHz with a maximum deviation of 75 kHz
explanation: This leaves guard bands between adjacent stations.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Transmission bandwidth of FM signals
stem: Wideband FM has a modulation index that is:
options: Much greater than 1, giving many significant sidebands
explanation: Its bandwidth is far greater than 2fm.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Transmission bandwidth of FM signals
stem: The number of significant sidebands in an FM spectrum increases with:
explanation: Sidebands whose Bessel coefficient exceeds about 0.01 are counted.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Transmission bandwidth of FM signals
stem: The deviation ratio of an FM system is defined as:
options: The maximum deviation divided by the maximum modulating frequency
explanation: For FM broadcast it is 75/15 = 5.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Transmission bandwidth of FM signals
stem: The FM improvement in SNR over AM comes at the cost of:
explanation: This is the classic bandwidth versus noise performance trade-off.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Transmission bandwidth of FM signals
stem: The threshold effect in FM reception means that below a certain input SNR:
options: The output SNR degrades very rapidly and the noise advantage is lost
explanation: FM demodulators using feedback can lower the threshold slightly.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Generation, detection, FM transmitters and receivers
stem: A direct method of FM generation uses:
options: A varactor diode or reactance modulator to vary the oscillator tank frequency
explanation: Its drawback is poor carrier frequency stability, needing AFC.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Generation, detection, FM transmitters and receivers
stem: The Armstrong method generates FM indirectly by:
options: Integrating the message, phase modulating a crystal carrier, then multiplying
explanation: Crystal control gives excellent carrier frequency stability.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Generation, detection, FM transmitters and receivers
stem: A frequency discriminator or slope detector demodulates FM by:
options: Converting frequency variations into amplitude variations, then envelope detecting
explanation: The Foster-Seeley and ratio detectors are balanced versions.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Generation, detection, FM transmitters and receivers
stem: A limiter stage in an FM receiver is used to:
options: Remove amplitude variations caused by noise before detection
explanation: This is the key to the noise immunity of FM.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Generation, detection, FM transmitters and receivers
stem: The standard intermediate frequency of an FM broadcast receiver is:
explanation: The higher IF gives better image rejection at VHF.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Generation, detection, FM transmitters and receivers
stem: A ratio detector is preferred over a Foster-Seeley discriminator because it:
options: Provides inherent amplitude limiting, reducing the need for a limiter stage
explanation: Its output is proportional to the ratio of the two diode voltages.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Generation, detection, FM transmitters and receivers
stem: A phase locked loop FM detector produces the demodulated output at:
options: The output of the loop filter driving the VCO
explanation: The VCO control voltage must track the instantaneous frequency.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Generation, detection, FM transmitters and receivers
stem: Pre-emphasis at an FM transmitter is used to:
options: Boost high frequency message components before modulation
explanation: A matching de-emphasis network at the receiver restores the balance.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Generation, detection, FM transmitters and receivers
stem: The standard pre-emphasis time constant used in FM broadcasting is:
options: 50 microseconds in most of the world, 75 in North America
explanation: It corresponds to a break frequency near 3.2 kHz.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Generation, detection, FM transmitters and receivers
stem: In stereo FM broadcasting the L-R difference signal is transmitted as:
options: A DSB-SC signal on a 38 kHz subcarrier with a 19 kHz pilot
explanation: Mono receivers simply ignore the subcarrier and reproduce L+R.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Generation, detection, FM transmitters and receivers
stem: Automatic frequency control in an FM receiver is used to:
options: Correct local oscillator drift by feeding back a DC error from the discriminator
explanation: It keeps the signal centred in the IF passband.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Frequency and Phase Modulation
stem: The capture effect in FM means that the receiver:
options: Suppresses the weaker of two co-channel signals almost entirely
explanation: A capture ratio of a few dB is typical of good receivers.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Frequency and Phase Modulation
stem: The total power in an FM signal is independent of the modulation index.
explanation: The constant envelope means power is only redistributed among the sidebands.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Transmission bandwidth of FM signals
stem: Carson's rule states that FM bandwidth equals twice the modulating frequency.
explanation: Carson's rule gives B = 2(delta f + fm), including the deviation.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Generation, detection, FM transmitters and receivers
stem:
Assertion (A): FM receivers include a limiter stage before the detector.
Reason (R): Noise mainly appears as amplitude variation, which the constant envelope FM signal does not carry.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Clipping the amplitude therefore removes most of the noise before demodulation.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Generation, detection, FM transmitters and receivers
stem:
Assertion (A): Pre-emphasis and de-emphasis improve the SNR of an FM system.
Reason (R): Noise power in FM detection increases with the square of the baseband frequency.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Boosting highs before transmission and cutting them after suppresses this noise.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

topic: Frequency and Phase Modulation
stem: Which statements comparing FM with AM are correct?
options: FM has a constant transmitted power
FM receivers are simpler than AM receivers
explanation: FM receivers are more complex, needing limiters and discriminators.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 2

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

topic: Linear block codes: encoder and decoder
stem: Error control coding improves reliability by:

explanation: The cost is extra bandwidth or lower information throughput.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Linear block codes: encoder and decoder
stem: An (n, k) linear block code has:
options: k message bits and n-k parity bits in each n-bit codeword
explanation: Its code rate is k/n.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Linear block codes: encoder and decoder
stem: A code is linear if:
options: The modulo-2 sum of any two codewords is also a codeword
explanation: This makes the all-zero word always a valid codeword.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Linear block codes: encoder and decoder
stem: The Hamming distance between two codewords is:
options: The number of bit positions in which they differ
explanation: Minimum distance determines the error handling capability.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Linear block codes: encoder and decoder
stem: A code with minimum Hamming distance dmin can correct up to:
explanation: It can detect up to dmin - 1 errors.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Linear block codes: encoder and decoder
stem: A (7,4) Hamming code has a minimum distance of 3, so it can:
options: Correct one error or detect two errors
explanation: It is the classic single error correcting block code.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Linear block codes: encoder and decoder
stem: A systematic block code is one in which:
options: The message bits appear unchanged within the codeword
explanation: This simplifies the decoder because message extraction is trivial.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Linear block codes: encoder and decoder
stem: The generator matrix G of an (n,k) linear block code has dimensions:
explanation: The codeword is c = mG with modulo-2 arithmetic.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Linear block codes: encoder and decoder
stem: The parity check matrix H of an (n,k) code satisfies:
explanation: This orthogonality is what makes syndrome decoding work.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Linear block codes: encoder and decoder
stem: The syndrome of a received vector r is computed as:
explanation: A zero syndrome means no detectable error occurred.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Linear block codes: encoder and decoder
stem: The syndrome of a received word depends on:
options: The error pattern only, not the transmitted codeword
explanation: This is what allows a small syndrome table to locate errors.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Linear block codes: encoder and decoder
stem: Standard array decoding of a linear block code selects:
options: The coset leader of minimum weight as the estimated error pattern
explanation: This implements maximum likelihood decoding for a BSC.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Linear block codes: encoder and decoder
stem: A single parity check code can:
options: Detect any odd number of errors but correct none
explanation: Its minimum distance is only 2.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Cyclic codes: encoder and syndrome calculator
stem: A cyclic code has the property that:
options: Any cyclic shift of a codeword is also a codeword
explanation: This structure allows very simple shift register implementations.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Cyclic codes: encoder and syndrome calculator
stem: A cyclic code is described by its:
options: Generator polynomial g(x), a factor of x^n + 1
explanation: The degree of g(x) equals the number of parity bits n-k.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Cyclic codes: encoder and syndrome calculator
stem: An (n,k) cyclic code has a generator polynomial of degree:
explanation: It generates the n-k parity check bits.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Cyclic codes: encoder and syndrome calculator
stem: A cyclic encoder is implemented using:
options: A linear feedback shift register with taps set by the generator polynomial
explanation: This makes hardware implementation extremely economical.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Cyclic codes: encoder and syndrome calculator
stem: In systematic cyclic encoding, the parity bits are obtained as:
options: The remainder of x^(n-k) m(x) divided by g(x)
explanation: The message is then shifted up and the remainder appended.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Cyclic codes: encoder and syndrome calculator
stem: The syndrome calculator for a cyclic code computes:
options: The remainder when the received polynomial is divided by g(x)
explanation: A zero remainder indicates a valid codeword.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Cyclic codes: encoder and syndrome calculator
stem: Cyclic redundancy check codes are used mainly for:
options: Powerful burst error detection in data links and storage
explanation: CRC-32 is used in Ethernet frames and ZIP files.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Cyclic codes: encoder and syndrome calculator
stem: A CRC with r parity bits can detect all burst errors of length:

source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Cyclic codes: encoder and syndrome calculator
stem: BCH and Reed-Solomon codes are important because they are:
options: Cyclic codes with a designed multiple error correcting capability
explanation: Reed-Solomon operates on symbols, making it excellent for burst errors.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Cyclic codes: encoder and syndrome calculator
stem: Reed-Solomon codes are particularly effective against burst errors because:
options: They operate on multi-bit symbols, so a burst affects few symbols
explanation: This is why they are used in CDs, DVDs and deep space links.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Convolutional codes
stem: A convolutional encoder differs from a block encoder in that its output depends on:

source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Convolutional codes
stem: The constraint length of a convolutional code refers to:
options: The number of input bits that influence each output bit
explanation: A longer constraint length gives better performance but harder decoding.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Convolutional codes
stem: A rate 1/2 convolutional encoder produces:
options: Two output bits for every input bit
explanation: Puncturing can raise the rate to 2/3 or 3/4 when needed.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Convolutional codes
stem: The Viterbi algorithm decodes convolutional codes by:
options: Finding the maximum likelihood path through the trellis diagram
explanation: Its complexity grows exponentially with the constraint length.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Convolutional codes
stem: A convolutional encoder with m memory elements has how many trellis states?
explanation: Each state corresponds to a distinct shift register content.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Convolutional codes
stem: The free distance of a convolutional code determines its:
options: Error correcting capability, analogous to dmin in block codes
explanation: A larger free distance gives greater coding gain.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Convolutional codes
stem: Soft decision Viterbi decoding outperforms hard decision by approximately:
explanation: It uses quantised reliability information rather than binary decisions.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Linear block codes: encoder and decoder
stem: A code with minimum distance 3 can correct one error.
explanation: Correction capability is floor((dmin - 1)/2) = 1.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Cyclic codes: encoder and syndrome calculator
stem: Every cyclic code is also a linear block code.
explanation: Cyclic codes are a structured subclass of linear block codes.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Convolutional codes
stem:
Assertion (A): The Viterbi algorithm is widely used for decoding convolutional codes.
Reason (R): It performs maximum likelihood sequence estimation over the code trellis efficiently.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Its complexity is manageable for constraint lengths up to about 9.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Cyclic codes: encoder and syndrome calculator
stem:
Assertion (A): Cyclic codes are attractive for hardware implementation.
Reason (R): Both encoding and syndrome computation reduce to polynomial division by shift registers.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: This requires only a handful of flip-flops and XOR gates.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Linear block codes: encoder and decoder
stem: Which statements about linear block codes are correct?
options: The all-zero word is always a codeword
The syndrome depends only on the error pattern
Minimum distance equals the minimum non-zero codeword weight
They can correct any number of errors
explanation: Error correcting capability is strictly limited by the minimum distance.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 4

topic: Microwave communication systems
