topic: Satellite and mobile communication systems
stem: Handover in a cellular network refers to:
options: Transferring an ongoing call from one base station to another as the user moves
explanation: Soft handover in CDMA connects to two cells simultaneously.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 5

topic: Satellite and mobile communication systems
stem: GSM uses which multiple access technique?
explanation: Each 200 kHz carrier is divided into eight time slots.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 5

topic: Satellite and mobile communication systems
stem: 4G LTE uses which downlink multiple access scheme?
explanation: The uplink uses SC-FDMA to reduce the peak to average power ratio.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 5

topic: Satellite and mobile communication systems
stem: MIMO technology improves wireless performance by:
options: Using multiple antennas to exploit spatial multiplexing and diversity
explanation: It multiplies capacity without extra bandwidth or power.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 5

topic: Optical fibre communication systems
stem: Single mode fibre suffers from intermodal dispersion.
explanation: Only one mode propagates, so intermodal dispersion is eliminated by definition.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 5

topic: Satellite and mobile communication systems
stem: A geostationary satellite appears stationary from a point on the earth.
explanation: Its 24 hour equatorial orbit matches the earth's rotation rate.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 5

topic: Satellite and mobile communication systems
stem:
Assertion (A): Cellular networks divide a service area into small cells.
Reason (R): Small cells allow the same frequencies to be reused at short distances, multiplying capacity.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Reducing cell size is the primary way operators increase subscriber density.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 5

topic: Optical fibre communication systems
stem:
Assertion (A): Optical fibre offers far higher capacity than copper cable.
Reason (R): Its enormous carrier frequency and very low attenuation support terabit rates over long spans.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Fibre is also immune to electromagnetic interference and crosstalk.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 5

topic: Optical fibre communication systems
stem: Which are advantages of optical fibre communication?
options: Simple and cheap splicing in the field
explanation: Fibre splicing needs precision fusion equipment and skilled technicians.
source: BEU syllabus — Analog & Digital Communication System, Unit 5

topic: MOSFET operation, threshold voltage, current and channel length modulation
stem: An n-channel MOSFET enters the strong inversion region when:
options: The gate to source voltage exceeds the threshold voltage
explanation: An inversion layer of electrons then forms beneath the gate oxide.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: MOSFET operation, threshold voltage, current and channel length modulation
stem: A MOSFET operates in the saturation region when:
explanation: The channel is pinched off near the drain end.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: MOSFET operation, threshold voltage, current and channel length modulation
stem: The saturation drain current of a long channel MOSFET is:
explanation: It is quadratic in the gate overdrive voltage.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: MOSFET operation, threshold voltage, current and channel length modulation
stem: In the linear or triode region, a MOSFET behaves approximately as:
explanation: Its on-resistance falls as the gate overdrive increases.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: MOSFET operation, threshold voltage, current and channel length modulation
stem: The threshold voltage of a MOSFET depends on:
options: Oxide thickness, substrate doping, gate material and fixed oxide charge
explanation: Threshold implants are used to adjust it during fabrication.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: MOSFET operation, threshold voltage, current and channel length modulation
stem: Channel length modulation causes the saturation current to:
options: Increase slightly with VDS, giving a finite output resistance
explanation: The effective channel shortens as the pinch-off point moves.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: MOSFET operation, threshold voltage, current and channel length modulation
stem: Channel length modulation is modelled in the current equation by the factor:
explanation: Lambda is inversely proportional to the channel length.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: MOSFET operation, threshold voltage, current and channel length modulation
stem: Sub-threshold conduction in a MOSFET occurs:
options: Below the threshold voltage, with current varying exponentially with VGS
explanation: It is the dominant leakage mechanism in modern low VT devices.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: MOSFET operation, threshold voltage, current and channel length modulation
stem: The sub-threshold slope of a MOSFET is fundamentally limited at room temperature to:
explanation: This kT/q limit constrains supply voltage scaling.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: MOSFET operation, threshold voltage, current and channel length modulation
stem: Carrier mobility in a MOSFET channel decreases with:
options: Increasing temperature and increasing vertical electric field
explanation: Velocity saturation further limits current in short devices.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: Body bias, short channel effects, MOS switch and capacitances
stem: The body effect in a MOSFET refers to:
options: An increase in threshold voltage when the source to body voltage is positive
explanation: It is governed by the body effect coefficient gamma.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: Body bias, short channel effects, MOS switch and capacitances
stem: The body effect degrades the performance of stacked transistors because:
options: Upper devices in the stack see a raised threshold voltage
explanation: Transistor sizing must compensate for the reduced drive.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: Body bias, short channel effects, MOS switch and capacitances
stem: Drain induced barrier lowering (DIBL) is a short channel effect that:
options: Reduces the threshold voltage as the drain voltage increases
explanation: It worsens off-state leakage in scaled devices.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: Body bias, short channel effects, MOS switch and capacitances
stem: Velocity saturation in short channel MOSFETs causes the drain current to become:
options: Approximately linear rather than quadratic in gate overdrive
explanation: Carrier velocity saturates at high lateral electric fields.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: Body bias, short channel effects, MOS switch and capacitances
stem: Hot carrier injection in a MOSFET results in:
options: Gradual threshold shift and degradation from carriers trapped in the oxide
explanation: Lightly doped drain structures reduce the peak field responsible.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: Body bias, short channel effects, MOS switch and capacitances
stem: An NMOS transistor used as a pass switch passes:
options: A strong 0 but a degraded 1, losing a threshold voltage
explanation: A PMOS device is complementary, passing a strong 1 and weak 0.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: Body bias, short channel effects, MOS switch and capacitances
stem: A CMOS transmission gate consists of:
options: An NMOS and a PMOS in parallel driven by complementary gate signals
explanation: It passes both logic levels without threshold degradation.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: Body bias, short channel effects, MOS switch and capacitances
stem: The gate to channel capacitance of a MOSFET in saturation is distributed approximately as:
options: Two thirds to the source and none to the drain
explanation: In the linear region it splits equally between source and drain.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: Body bias, short channel effects, MOS switch and capacitances
stem: Overlap capacitance in a MOSFET arises from:
options: The gate extending over the source and drain diffusions
explanation: It is a fixed parasitic that does not scale with the operating region.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: Body bias, short channel effects, MOS switch and capacitances
stem: Junction capacitance of a MOSFET drain region is:
options: Voltage dependent, decreasing as the reverse bias increases
explanation: It contributes significantly to the self loading of a gate.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: CMOS layout elements, parasitics, design rules and SPICE characterisation
stem: In a standard CMOS layout, the NMOS transistors are placed:
options: In the p-substrate or p-well, near the ground rail
explanation: PMOS devices sit in the n-well near the VDD rail.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: CMOS layout elements, parasitics, design rules and SPICE characterisation
stem: A well tap or substrate contact is provided in a layout to:
options: Bias the well or substrate firmly, preventing latch-up
explanation: Frequent taps lower the parasitic well and substrate resistance.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: CMOS layout elements, parasitics, design rules and SPICE characterisation
stem: Latch-up in a CMOS circuit is caused by:
options: Triggering of the parasitic PNPN thyristor structure between well and substrate
explanation: It produces a destructive low impedance path from VDD to ground.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: CMOS layout elements, parasitics, design rules and SPICE characterisation
stem: Lambda based design rules express all dimensions in terms of:
options: A single scalable parameter lambda, making layouts process portable
explanation: Micron rules give better area efficiency for a specific process.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: CMOS layout elements, parasitics, design rules and SPICE characterisation
stem: A via in an integrated circuit layout is used to:
options: Connect metal layers on different levels
explanation: A contact instead connects metal to diffusion or polysilicon.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: CMOS layout elements, parasitics, design rules and SPICE characterisation
stem: The stick diagram of a CMOS gate is used to:
options: Plan the relative placement and connectivity before detailed layout
explanation: It captures topology without exact dimensions.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: CMOS layout elements, parasitics, design rules and SPICE characterisation
stem: Euler path traversal in CMOS layout is used to:
options: Find a gate ordering that allows uninterrupted diffusion, minimising area
explanation: A common Euler path in both networks gives the most compact cell.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: CMOS layout elements, parasitics, design rules and SPICE characterisation
stem: Interconnect parasitic resistance and capacitance in deep submicron designs:
explanation: Wire delay scales worse than gate delay with technology shrink.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: CMOS layout elements, parasitics, design rules and SPICE characterisation
stem: DRC and LVS checks in the VLSI design flow verify respectively:
options: Geometric manufacturability and layout to schematic equivalence
explanation: Both must pass before tapeout.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: CMOS layout elements, parasitics, design rules and SPICE characterisation
stem: SPICE parameter extraction from measured I-V characteristics is used to:
options: Fit the model parameters such as VT, k and lambda to real devices
explanation: Accurate models are essential for reliable circuit simulation.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: Body bias, short channel effects, MOS switch and capacitances
stem: A CMOS transmission gate passes both logic 0 and logic 1 without degradation.
explanation: The parallel NMOS and PMOS devices complement each other's weaknesses.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: MOSFET operation, threshold voltage, current and channel length modulation
stem: Channel length modulation makes the MOSFET output resistance infinite in saturation.
explanation: It causes current to rise with VDS, giving a finite output resistance.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: CMOS layout elements, parasitics, design rules and SPICE characterisation
stem:
Assertion (A): Substrate and well taps are placed liberally throughout a CMOS layout.
Reason (R): They reduce the parasitic resistance that could bias the vertical bipolar structures into conduction.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: This is the primary defence against destructive latch-up.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: Body bias, short channel effects, MOS switch and capacitances
stem:
Assertion (A): Short channel effects limit the scaling of MOSFETs.
Reason (R): DIBL and velocity saturation degrade threshold control and current drive as length shrinks.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: FinFET and gate-all-around structures were introduced to restore electrostatic control.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: Body bias, short channel effects, MOS switch and capacitances
stem: Which are short channel effects in MOSFETs?
explanation: Body effect occurs in long channel devices too and is not a short channel phenomenon.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 1

topic: CMOS inverter static characteristics, noise margin and supply scaling
stem: A CMOS inverter consists of:
options: A PMOS pull-up and an NMOS pull-down with common gate and drain
explanation: Exactly one device conducts strongly in each steady state.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: CMOS inverter static characteristics, noise margin and supply scaling
stem: The static power dissipation of an ideal CMOS inverter is:
options: Essentially zero, limited only by leakage
explanation: No direct path exists from VDD to ground in either steady state.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: CMOS inverter static characteristics, noise margin and supply scaling
stem: The switching threshold VM of a CMOS inverter is the input voltage at which:
options: The output equals the input, with both transistors in saturation
explanation: It depends on the ratio of PMOS to NMOS drive strengths.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: CMOS inverter static characteristics, noise margin and supply scaling
stem: To set the switching threshold of a CMOS inverter at VDD/2, the PMOS is made:
options: Wider than the NMOS, typically 2 to 3 times
explanation: Hole mobility is roughly two to three times lower than electron mobility.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: CMOS inverter static characteristics, noise margin and supply scaling
stem: The noise margin high NMH of a logic gate is defined as:
explanation: NML is correspondingly VIL minus VOL.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: CMOS inverter static characteristics, noise margin and supply scaling
stem: A CMOS inverter has excellent noise margins because:
options: Its output swings rail to rail and the transfer curve is very steep
explanation: A symmetric inverter has noise margins close to VDD/2.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: CMOS inverter static characteristics, noise margin and supply scaling
stem: VIL and VIH on the voltage transfer characteristic are defined as the points where:
explanation: Beyond these points the gate provides signal restoration.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: CMOS inverter static characteristics, noise margin and supply scaling
stem: Process variation affects the CMOS inverter mainly by:
options: Shifting the switching threshold and altering the drive strengths
explanation: Corner analysis with SS, TT and FF models covers the spread.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: CMOS inverter static characteristics, noise margin and supply scaling
stem: Reducing the supply voltage of a CMOS gate:
options: Reduces dynamic power quadratically but increases delay
explanation: Voltage scaling is the single most effective low power technique.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: CMOS inverter static characteristics, noise margin and supply scaling
stem: Sub-threshold operation of CMOS logic at very low supply voltage gives:
options: Minimum energy per operation but very slow speed
explanation: It suits ultra low power sensors and medical implants.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Complementary CMOS design, propagation delay and Elmore delay model
stem: In complementary static CMOS logic, the pull-up network is:
options: The dual of the pull-down network, built from PMOS devices
explanation: Series in one network becomes parallel in the other.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Complementary CMOS design, propagation delay and Elmore delay model
stem: A static CMOS NAND gate has its NMOS transistors:
options: In parallel and PMOS in series
In series and the PMOS transistors in parallel
explanation: A NOR gate is the exact opposite arrangement.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Complementary CMOS design, propagation delay and Elmore delay model
stem: A CMOS NOR gate is generally slower than a NAND gate of the same fan-in because:
options: The series PMOS devices must be made very wide to match the drive
explanation: NAND based logic is therefore preferred in static CMOS design.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Complementary CMOS design, propagation delay and Elmore delay model
stem: The propagation delay of a CMOS gate is approximately proportional to:
options: The load capacitance divided by the drive current
explanation: Increasing device width raises drive but also self loading.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Complementary CMOS design, propagation delay and Elmore delay model
stem: The Elmore delay model estimates RC network delay as:
options: The product of all R and C
The sum over nodes of the resistance shared with the source times the node capacitance
explanation: It gives a first order estimate of distributed interconnect delay.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Complementary CMOS design, propagation delay and Elmore delay model
stem: The delay of a uniform RC line of length L increases with:
explanation: Repeater insertion makes the delay linear in length instead.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Complementary CMOS design, propagation delay and Elmore delay model
stem: Buffer or repeater insertion on a long wire is used to:
options: Break the quadratic RC delay into shorter linear segments
explanation: An optimum number and size of repeaters minimises total delay.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Complementary CMOS design, propagation delay and Elmore delay model
stem: Transistor sizing in a chain of inverters driving a large load is optimal when:
options: Each stage is larger than the previous by a fixed factor near e
explanation: A practical factor of 3 to 4 is used to balance delay and area.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Complementary CMOS design, propagation delay and Elmore delay model
stem: Logical effort of a gate quantifies:
options: Its drive capability relative to an inverter with equal input capacitance
explanation: A 2-input NAND has a logical effort of 4/3.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Complementary CMOS design, propagation delay and Elmore delay model
stem: In the logical effort method, path delay is minimised when:
options: The stage effort is equal in every stage of the path
Effort is concentrated in one stage
explanation: The optimum stage effort is the Nth root of the path effort.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Power consumption, low power techniques, logical effort and ratioed logic
stem: Dynamic switching power in CMOS is given by:
explanation: Alpha is the switching activity factor.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Power consumption, low power techniques, logical effort and ratioed logic
stem: Short circuit power in a CMOS gate arises because:
options: Both transistors conduct briefly during the input transition
explanation: Fast input slopes minimise this component.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Power consumption, low power techniques, logical effort and ratioed logic
stem: Static leakage power in modern CMOS is dominated by:
options: Sub-threshold and gate oxide tunnelling currents
explanation: High-k dielectrics were introduced to curb gate tunnelling.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Power consumption, low power techniques, logical effort and ratioed logic
stem: Clock gating reduces power by:
options: Disabling the clock to inactive blocks, cutting switching activity
explanation: The clock network is often the largest single power consumer.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Power consumption, low power techniques, logical effort and ratioed logic
stem: Power gating differs from clock gating because it:
options: Disconnects the supply from idle blocks, eliminating leakage as well
explanation: Header or footer sleep transistors implement the switch.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Power consumption, low power techniques, logical effort and ratioed logic
stem: Multi-VT design assigns high threshold transistors to:
options: Non-critical paths, to cut leakage without hurting speed
explanation: Low VT devices are reserved for timing critical paths.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Power consumption, low power techniques, logical effort and ratioed logic
stem: Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling saves energy by:
options: Lowering both supply voltage and clock rate when full performance is not needed
explanation: Energy savings are roughly cubic in the scaling factor.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Power consumption, low power techniques, logical effort and ratioed logic
stem: Ratioed logic such as pseudo-NMOS differs from static CMOS in that it:
options: Uses a single always-on PMOS load, dissipating static power
explanation: Its output low level depends on the ratio of pull-up to pull-down strength.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Power consumption, low power techniques, logical effort and ratioed logic
stem: The main advantage of pseudo-NMOS logic over static CMOS is:
options: Far fewer transistors and lower input capacitance for wide fan-in gates
explanation: Its VOL is not zero, degrading the low noise margin.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Power consumption, low power techniques, logical effort and ratioed logic
stem: Energy delay product is used as a design metric because it:
options: Balances the trade-off between speed and energy consumption
explanation: Optimising energy alone would drive the design to impractical slowness.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: CMOS inverter static characteristics, noise margin and supply scaling
stem: A static CMOS inverter dissipates negligible power in steady state.
explanation: There is no conducting path from supply to ground in either logic state.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Complementary CMOS design, propagation delay and Elmore delay model
stem: A CMOS NOR gate is generally faster than a NAND gate of the same fan-in.
explanation: The series PMOS stack in a NOR gate makes it slower for the same area.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Power consumption, low power techniques, logical effort and ratioed logic
stem:
Assertion (A): Supply voltage scaling is the most effective low power technique.
Reason (R): Dynamic power depends on the square of the supply voltage.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The penalty is increased gate delay, which limits how far voltage can be reduced.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: CMOS inverter static characteristics, noise margin and supply scaling
stem:
Assertion (A): The PMOS transistor in a CMOS inverter is made wider than the NMOS.
Reason (R): Hole mobility is about two to three times lower than electron mobility.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Equal drive strengths give a symmetric transfer curve and equal rise and fall times.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Power consumption, low power techniques, logical effort and ratioed logic
stem: Which techniques reduce power consumption in CMOS circuits?
explanation: Higher switching activity directly increases dynamic power.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 2

topic: Pseudo-NMOS, DCVSL, pass transistor logic and transmission gate logic
stem: A pseudo-NMOS inverter uses:
options: A grounded gate PMOS as a permanently on load with an NMOS pull-down network
explanation: It halves the transistor count of a static CMOS gate.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Pseudo-NMOS, DCVSL, pass transistor logic and transmission gate logic
stem: The main drawback of pseudo-NMOS logic is:
options: Static power dissipation whenever the output is low
explanation: The load PMOS conducts continuously in that state.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Pseudo-NMOS, DCVSL, pass transistor logic and transmission gate logic
stem: The output low voltage of a pseudo-NMOS gate is determined by:
options: The strength ratio of the NMOS network to the PMOS load
explanation: This ratioed behaviour degrades the low noise margin.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Pseudo-NMOS, DCVSL, pass transistor logic and transmission gate logic
stem: Differential cascode voltage switch logic (DCVSL) produces:
options: Both true and complementary outputs using cross coupled PMOS latching
explanation: It is ratioed but has no static power dissipation.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Pseudo-NMOS, DCVSL, pass transistor logic and transmission gate logic
stem: An advantage of DCVSL over static CMOS is:
options: Complementary outputs available without extra inverters, useful for XOR functions
explanation: Its drawback is the need for both true and complement inputs.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Pseudo-NMOS, DCVSL, pass transistor logic and transmission gate logic
stem: Pass transistor logic implements functions by:
options: Steering input signals through transistors to the output node
explanation: It can realise a 2:1 multiplexer with only two transistors.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Pseudo-NMOS, DCVSL, pass transistor logic and transmission gate logic
stem: The main problem with NMOS-only pass transistor logic is:
options: Threshold voltage drop on a logic 1 causing static current in the next stage
explanation: A level restoring PMOS feedback transistor fixes this.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Pseudo-NMOS, DCVSL, pass transistor logic and transmission gate logic
stem: Complementary pass transistor logic (CPL) uses:
options: Dual rail NMOS pass networks with output inverters for level restoration
explanation: It gives high speed for arithmetic circuits like adders.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Pseudo-NMOS, DCVSL, pass transistor logic and transmission gate logic
stem: A 2:1 multiplexer built from transmission gates requires:
options: Two transmission gates driven by complementary select signals
explanation: Each transmission gate is two transistors.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Pseudo-NMOS, DCVSL, pass transistor logic and transmission gate logic
stem: Cascading many pass transistor stages is undesirable because:
options: The series RC delay grows quadratically with the number of stages
explanation: Buffers must be inserted every three or four stages.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Dynamic CMOS design, speed and power considerations
stem: A dynamic CMOS gate operates in two phases known as:
explanation: A clock signal controls the transition between them.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Dynamic CMOS design, speed and power considerations
stem: During the precharge phase of a dynamic gate:
options: The PMOS precharge device pulls the output high while the NMOS foot is off
explanation: The evaluate transistor prevents a direct path to ground.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Dynamic CMOS design, speed and power considerations
stem: The main advantage of dynamic CMOS logic is:
options: Fewer transistors and lower input capacitance, giving higher speed
explanation: Only the NMOS pull-down network plus two clocked devices are needed.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Dynamic CMOS design, speed and power considerations
stem: Charge leakage in a dynamic gate causes:
options: Loss of the stored high level if the clock period is too long
explanation: A small keeper transistor restores the leaked charge.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Dynamic CMOS design, speed and power considerations
stem: Charge sharing in a dynamic gate occurs when:
options: The output charge redistributes onto internal node capacitances
explanation: Precharging the internal nodes prevents the resulting voltage droop.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Dynamic CMOS design, speed and power considerations
stem: Dynamic gates cannot be directly cascaded because:
options: The brief high state of an input during precharge can falsely discharge the next gate
explanation: Domino logic solves this by adding a static inverter.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Dynamic CMOS design, speed and power considerations
stem: Clock feedthrough in a dynamic gate refers to:
options: Coupling of the clock edge to the output through gate overlap capacitance
explanation: It can push the output above VDD or below ground briefly.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Dynamic CMOS design, speed and power considerations
stem: Dynamic logic tends to consume more clock power than static logic because:
options: The output precharges and discharges on every clock cycle regardless of data
explanation: Its switching activity factor approaches unity.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Dynamic CMOS design, speed and power considerations
stem: A keeper transistor in a dynamic gate is deliberately made weak so that:
options: The pull-down network can still overpower it during a valid evaluation
explanation: A strong keeper would reintroduce ratioed behaviour and slow the gate.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Domino logic, C2MOS, TSPC registers and NORA CMOS
stem: Domino logic adds to each dynamic gate:
options: A static CMOS inverter at the output, allowing cascading
explanation: Inputs to the following stage then stay low during precharge.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Domino logic, C2MOS, TSPC registers and NORA CMOS
stem: A fundamental limitation of standard domino logic is that it:
explanation: Dual rail domino or NP domino overcomes this restriction.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Domino logic, C2MOS, TSPC registers and NORA CMOS
stem: Multiple output domino logic is attractive because it:
options: Shares one pull-down network to produce several related outputs, as in carry chains
explanation: It is widely used in high speed adder carry generation.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Domino logic, C2MOS, TSPC registers and NORA CMOS
stem: C2MOS logic uses a clocked CMOS structure that:
options: Is insensitive to clock skew when driven by a two phase non-overlapping clock
explanation: It provides a robust dynamic latch structure.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Domino logic, C2MOS, TSPC registers and NORA CMOS
stem: NORA CMOS logic alternates:
options: N-type and P-type dynamic blocks so that they can be cascaded
explanation: No race condition occurs with proper alternation.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Domino logic, C2MOS, TSPC registers and NORA CMOS
stem: A TSPC register is attractive because it:
options: Requires only a single clock phase, avoiding clock skew between phases
explanation: TSPC stands for true single phase clocked logic.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Domino logic, C2MOS, TSPC registers and NORA CMOS
stem: The setup time of a flip-flop is the interval during which the data must be:
options: Stable before the active clock edge
explanation: Hold time is the corresponding requirement after the edge.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Domino logic, C2MOS, TSPC registers and NORA CMOS
stem: Clock skew between two sequential elements can cause:
options: Hold time violations if the receiving clock arrives too late
explanation: Balanced H-tree clock distribution minimises skew.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Domino logic, C2MOS, TSPC registers and NORA CMOS
stem: Metastability in a flip-flop occurs when:
options: Setup or hold time is violated and the output hovers between levels
explanation: Synchroniser chains reduce the probability of failure.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Domino logic, C2MOS, TSPC registers and NORA CMOS
stem: Dual rail domino logic overcomes the non-inverting limitation by:
options: Computing both the function and its complement in parallel networks
explanation: The cost is roughly double the area and power.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Domino logic, C2MOS, TSPC registers and NORA CMOS
stem: Pipelining a domino logic datapath improves throughput by:
options: Overlapping evaluation of successive stages using skewed clock phases
explanation: Careful clock design is essential to avoid race conditions.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Dynamic CMOS design, speed and power considerations
stem: Dynamic CMOS gates require a clock signal to operate.
explanation: The clock defines the precharge and evaluate phases.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Domino logic, C2MOS, TSPC registers and NORA CMOS
stem: Standard domino logic can implement inverting functions directly.
explanation: The output inverter makes each domino stage non-inverting overall.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Dynamic CMOS design, speed and power considerations
stem:
Assertion (A): A keeper transistor is added to dynamic logic gates.
Reason (R): Sub-threshold leakage would otherwise discharge the dynamic node during a long evaluate phase.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The keeper is sized weak so it does not fight a genuine pull-down.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Pseudo-NMOS, DCVSL, pass transistor logic and transmission gate logic
stem:
Assertion (A): NMOS pass transistor logic needs a level restoring transistor.
Reason (R): An NMOS device passes a logic high degraded by one threshold voltage.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The degraded level would cause static current in the following CMOS gate.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Dynamic CMOS design, speed and power considerations
stem: Which are disadvantages of dynamic CMOS logic compared with static CMOS?
options: Sensitivity to charge leakage and charge sharing
Higher clock power due to activity factor near one
explanation: Dynamic logic actually uses fewer transistors than static CMOS.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 3

topic: Design of adders and arithmetic circuits
stem: A full adder produces:
options: A sum and a carry out from three input bits
explanation: Sum is the XOR of all three inputs.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Design of adders and arithmetic circuits
stem: A ripple carry adder is slow because:
options: The carry must propagate serially through every stage
explanation: Its worst case delay grows linearly with word length.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Design of adders and arithmetic circuits
stem: A carry look-ahead adder speeds up addition by:
options: Computing generate and propagate signals to form carries in parallel
explanation: Its delay grows logarithmically with the word length.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Design of adders and arithmetic circuits
stem: The carry generate signal in a look-ahead adder is defined as:
explanation: The propagate signal Pi is Ai XOR Bi or Ai OR Bi.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Design of adders and arithmetic circuits
stem: A carry select adder achieves speed by:
options: Computing sums for both possible carry inputs and selecting when the carry arrives
explanation: It trades roughly double the area for reduced delay.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Design of adders and arithmetic circuits
stem: A carry skip (carry bypass) adder improves speed by:
options: Bypassing groups of bits when all their propagate signals are true
explanation: It offers a good compromise between area and delay.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Design of adders and arithmetic circuits
stem: A mirror adder circuit is popular in VLSI because it:
options: Uses 28 transistors with a symmetric layout and shared carry path
explanation: The carry output is deliberately made fast because it is on the critical path.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Design of adders and arithmetic circuits
stem: In an adder chain, the carry path is optimised more aggressively than the sum path because:
options: The carry is on the critical path through all stages
explanation: Sum outputs are computed only once per stage.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Design of adders and arithmetic circuits
stem: A parallel prefix adder such as Kogge-Stone provides:
options: Logarithmic depth carry computation at the cost of high wiring complexity
explanation: Brent-Kung trades some depth for far fewer wires.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Design of adders and arithmetic circuits
stem: A Manchester carry chain implements carry propagation using:
options: Pass transistors controlled by the propagate signals in a dynamic chain
explanation: It is compact and fast for moderate group sizes.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Multipliers and shifters
stem: An array multiplier computes a product by:
options: Generating partial products and summing them in a regular array of adders
explanation: Its regular structure makes layout straightforward.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Multipliers and shifters
stem: A Wallace tree multiplier reduces delay by:
options: Compressing partial products with carry save adders in a logarithmic tree
explanation: A final fast carry propagate adder produces the result.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Multipliers and shifters
stem: A carry save adder is useful in multipliers because it:
options: Adds three numbers producing sum and carry vectors without carry propagation
explanation: Carry propagation is deferred to a single final stage.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Multipliers and shifters
stem: Booth encoding is used in multipliers to:
options: Reduce the number of partial products by recoding the multiplier bits
explanation: Radix-4 modified Booth halves the number of partial products.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Multipliers and shifters
stem: A barrel shifter performs:
options: An arbitrary shift or rotate in a single operation using multiplexer stages
explanation: An n-bit barrel shifter uses log2(n) multiplexer stages.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Multipliers and shifters
stem: A logarithmic shifter for 32 bits requires how many multiplexer stages?
explanation: Each stage shifts by a power of two.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Multipliers and shifters
stem: An arithmetic right shift differs from a logical right shift because it:
options: Replicates the sign bit into the vacated positions
explanation: This preserves the value of a signed two's complement number.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Multipliers and shifters
stem: Pipelining a multiplier increases throughput by:
options: Inserting registers between stages so several operations overlap
explanation: Latency in cycles increases while throughput improves.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Multipliers and shifters
stem: A 4:2 compressor used in multiplier trees:
options: Reduces four partial product bits to two with regular structure and low delay
explanation: Its regularity simplifies layout compared with a pure Wallace tree.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: CMOS memory design: SRAM and DRAM
stem: A standard SRAM cell consists of:
options: Six transistors: two cross coupled inverters and two access transistors
explanation: It retains data as long as power is applied.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: CMOS memory design: SRAM and DRAM
stem: A DRAM cell consists of:
options: One access transistor and one storage capacitor
explanation: Its very high density comes at the cost of needing refresh.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: CMOS memory design: SRAM and DRAM
stem: DRAM requires periodic refresh because:
options: Charge stored on the cell capacitor leaks away over milliseconds
explanation: Typical refresh intervals are 32 or 64 milliseconds.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: CMOS memory design: SRAM and DRAM
stem: Reading a DRAM cell is destructive, which means:
options: The data must be written back after every read operation
explanation: The sense amplifier automatically performs the restore.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: CMOS memory design: SRAM and DRAM
stem: A sense amplifier in a memory array is used to:
options: Detect and amplify the small differential bit line voltage quickly
explanation: Differential operation gives good common mode noise rejection.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: CMOS memory design: SRAM and DRAM
stem: The cell ratio of an SRAM cell must be chosen to ensure:
options: Read stability, preventing the stored bit from flipping during a read
explanation: The pull-up ratio governs write ability in the opposite direction.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: CMOS memory design: SRAM and DRAM
stem: Bit line precharging before a memory access is performed to:
options: Equalise the bit lines so the sense amplifier sees a clean differential
explanation: Precharge is typically to VDD or VDD/2.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: CMOS memory design: SRAM and DRAM
stem: A row decoder in a memory array:
options: Activates one word line based on the row address bits
explanation: Column decoders select which bit lines reach the output.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: CMOS memory design: SRAM and DRAM
stem: SRAM is used for cache memory rather than DRAM because it is:
options: Much faster and needs no refresh
explanation: Its six transistor cell makes it far less dense than DRAM.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: CMOS memory design: SRAM and DRAM
stem: A folded bit line architecture in DRAM is used to:
options: Improve noise immunity by placing the reference cell on an adjacent line
explanation: Both bit lines then experience the same coupling noise.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: CMOS memory design: SRAM and DRAM
stem: A trench or stacked capacitor is used in modern DRAM to:
options: Obtain sufficient storage capacitance in a very small silicon footprint
explanation: Adequate cell capacitance is essential for reliable sensing.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: CMOS memory design: SRAM and DRAM
stem: SRAM requires periodic refresh to retain data.
explanation: Only DRAM needs refresh; SRAM holds data as long as power is applied.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Design of adders and arithmetic circuits
stem: The carry path is the critical path in a ripple carry adder.
explanation: The carry must ripple serially through every full adder stage.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Multipliers and shifters
stem:
Assertion (A): Booth encoding is widely used in high speed multipliers.
Reason (R): It halves the number of partial products that must be summed.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Fewer partial products means a shallower reduction tree and lower delay.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: CMOS memory design: SRAM and DRAM
stem:
Assertion (A): DRAM reads are followed by an automatic write-back.
Reason (R): Reading a DRAM cell shares its stored charge with the bit line and destroys the data.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The sense amplifier restores the full level to the cell after sensing.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: Design of adders and arithmetic circuits
stem: Which adder architectures are faster than a ripple carry adder?
explanation: A serial adder processes one bit per clock cycle and is far slower.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 4

topic: BiCMOS logic: structure and static behaviour
stem: BiCMOS technology combines:
options: Bipolar transistors and CMOS devices on the same chip
explanation: It aims to obtain the strengths of both technologies.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: BiCMOS logic: structure and static behaviour
stem: In a typical BiCMOS inverter, the CMOS section provides:
options: The logic function and high input impedance
explanation: The bipolar output stage supplies the large drive current.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: BiCMOS logic: structure and static behaviour
stem: The bipolar output transistors in a BiCMOS gate provide:
options: High current drive for large capacitive loads
explanation: Their transconductance far exceeds that of MOS devices.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: BiCMOS logic: structure and static behaviour
stem: The output voltage swing of a conventional BiCMOS gate is limited to:
options: VDD minus VBE at the high level and VBE above ground at the low level
explanation: This reduced swing degrades the noise margin at low supply voltages.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: BiCMOS logic: structure and static behaviour
stem: Full swing BiCMOS circuits add:
options: MOS pull-up and pull-down devices in parallel with the bipolar output stage
explanation: This restores rail to rail levels at the cost of extra transistors.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: BiCMOS logic: structure and static behaviour
stem: Base charge removal networks are included in BiCMOS gates to:
options: Turn the output bipolar transistors off quickly
explanation: Stored base charge would otherwise slow the turn-off transition considerably.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: BiCMOS logic: structure and static behaviour
stem: The static power dissipation of a well designed BiCMOS gate is:
options: Low, similar to CMOS, since no DC path exists in steady state
explanation: Base leakage and resistor paths contribute a small amount.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: BiCMOS logic: structure and static behaviour
stem: Fabricating BiCMOS requires:
options: More masks and process steps than pure CMOS, raising cost
explanation: Typically 3 to 5 extra masks are needed for the bipolar devices.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: BiCMOS logic: structure and static behaviour
stem: The transconductance of a bipolar transistor compared with a MOSFET at the same current is:
options: Much higher, because gm equals Ic/VT
explanation: This gives bipolar devices superior drive per unit area.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Dynamic behaviour, delay and power consumption in BiCMOS
stem: BiCMOS logic shows a clear delay advantage over CMOS when:
options: Driving large capacitive loads such as long buses
explanation: For small loads, CMOS is actually faster.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Dynamic behaviour, delay and power consumption in BiCMOS
stem: The delay of a BiCMOS gate versus load capacitance has a slope that is:
options: Much flatter than CMOS, so it degrades slowly with load
explanation: The two curves cross at a characteristic load capacitance.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Dynamic behaviour, delay and power consumption in BiCMOS
stem: At small load capacitance, a BiCMOS gate is slower than a CMOS gate because of:
options: The base-emitter turn-on delay and internal parasitic capacitances
explanation: The bipolar overhead is only worthwhile for large loads.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Dynamic behaviour, delay and power consumption in BiCMOS
stem: The dynamic power of a BiCMOS gate is affected by:
options: The reduced voltage swing, which lowers CV squared f
explanation: Base drive current adds an additional power component, however.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Dynamic behaviour, delay and power consumption in BiCMOS
stem: The storage time of the output bipolar transistor in BiCMOS is reduced by:
options: Preventing the transistor from entering deep saturation
explanation: Schottky clamps serve the same purpose in bipolar logic.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Dynamic behaviour, delay and power consumption in BiCMOS
stem: BiCMOS is well suited to clock driver circuits because they:
options: Must drive very large capacitive loads with minimum skew
explanation: Bus drivers and I/O buffers are similar applications.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Dynamic behaviour, delay and power consumption in BiCMOS
stem: The crossover load capacitance between CMOS and BiCMOS delay curves marks:
options: The load beyond which BiCMOS becomes the faster choice
explanation: It typically lies in the range of a fraction of a picofarad.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Dynamic behaviour, delay and power consumption in BiCMOS
stem: BiCMOS becomes less attractive at low supply voltages because:
options: The fixed VBE drop consumes an increasing fraction of the available swing
explanation: This is why BiCMOS declined as supplies scaled below 3 V.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Dynamic behaviour, delay and power consumption in BiCMOS
stem: A BiNMOS gate uses:
options: A bipolar pull-up with an NMOS pull-down for a full low level swing
explanation: It improves the low level noise margin over conventional BiCMOS.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Comparison with CMOS and bipolar logic, applications and VLSI design flow
stem: Compared with pure bipolar ECL, BiCMOS offers:
options: Much lower static power at somewhat lower speed
explanation: ECL dissipates continuous current in its current steering pairs.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Comparison with CMOS and bipolar logic, applications and VLSI design flow
stem: Compared with pure CMOS, BiCMOS offers:
options: Higher drive capability at the cost of process complexity and area
explanation: It found use in mixed signal and high drive applications.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Comparison with CMOS and bipolar logic, applications and VLSI design flow
stem: A major present day application of BiCMOS technology is:
options: RF and analogue front ends where bipolar devices give superior gain and noise
explanation: SiGe BiCMOS is widely used in wireless transceivers.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Comparison with CMOS and bipolar logic, applications and VLSI design flow
stem: The Y chart of VLSI design describes:
options: Behavioural, structural and physical domains at several levels of abstraction
explanation: Design proceeds by moving inward across these three axes.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Comparison with CMOS and bipolar logic, applications and VLSI design flow
stem: An ASIC design flow typically begins with:
options: RTL description in an HDL, followed by synthesis
explanation: Synthesis maps the RTL onto a standard cell library.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Comparison with CMOS and bipolar logic, applications and VLSI design flow
stem: Static timing analysis is used to:
options: Verify that all paths meet setup and hold requirements without simulation vectors
explanation: It is exhaustive over all paths, unlike dynamic simulation.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Comparison with CMOS and bipolar logic, applications and VLSI design flow
stem: Place and route in the physical design flow determines:
options: The locations of standard cells and the wiring between them
explanation: Timing closure is achieved by iterating with the timing analyser.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Comparison with CMOS and bipolar logic, applications and VLSI design flow
stem: Design for testability techniques such as scan chains:
options: Convert flip-flops into a shift register to control and observe internal nodes
explanation: Built-in self test generates and checks patterns on chip.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Comparison with CMOS and bipolar logic, applications and VLSI design flow
stem: A standard cell library provides:
options: Pre-characterised logic gates of fixed height with timing and power models
explanation: Fixed cell height allows automatic row based placement.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Comparison with CMOS and bipolar logic, applications and VLSI design flow
stem: An FPGA differs from an ASIC in that it is:
options: Field programmable with no fabrication needed, at the cost of speed and density
explanation: ASICs win on unit cost, power and performance at high volume.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Comparison with CMOS and bipolar logic, applications and VLSI design flow
stem: Moore's law as originally stated predicted that:
options: The number of transistors on a chip would double roughly every two years
explanation: Its economic and physical limits are now being reached.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Comparison with CMOS and bipolar logic, applications and VLSI design flow
stem: Signal integrity issues in deep submicron design include:
options: Crosstalk, IR drop and electromigration in the interconnect
explanation: Shielding, wider power grids and current limits address them.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Dynamic behaviour, delay and power consumption in BiCMOS
stem: BiCMOS is faster than CMOS for all load capacitances.
explanation: For small loads CMOS is faster; BiCMOS wins only beyond a crossover capacitance.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: BiCMOS logic: structure and static behaviour
stem: A conventional BiCMOS gate has a full rail to rail output swing.
explanation: The output is limited by the base-emitter voltage drops of the bipolar devices.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Dynamic behaviour, delay and power consumption in BiCMOS
stem:
Assertion (A): BiCMOS lost popularity as supply voltages scaled down.
Reason (R): The fixed VBE drop consumes a growing fraction of a shrinking supply voltage.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Noise margins and swing become unacceptable at supplies near 1 V.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: BiCMOS logic: structure and static behaviour
stem:
Assertion (A): BiCMOS gates are excellent for driving large capacitive loads.
Reason (R): The bipolar output stage supplies far more current per unit area than a MOSFET.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: This makes them ideal for clock and bus driver applications.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Comparison with CMOS and bipolar logic, applications and VLSI design flow
stem: Which are advantages of BiCMOS over pure CMOS?
options: Superior analogue and RF device characteristics
explanation: BiCMOS fabrication requires additional masks and steps, making it more expensive.
source: BEU syllabus — Introduction to VLSI Design, Unit 5

topic: Public speaking
stem: The first step in preparing an effective speech is to:
options: Analyse the audience and define the purpose
explanation: Content and style must suit the listeners' needs.
source: BEU syllabus — Professional Skill Development, Unit 1

topic: Public speaking
stem: Glossophobia refers to:
explanation: Preparation and practice are the best remedies.
source: BEU syllabus — Professional Skill Development, Unit 1

topic: Public speaking
stem: An effective speech opening should:
options: Capture attention and state the purpose clearly
explanation: A question, story or striking statistic works well.
source: BEU syllabus — Professional Skill Development, Unit 1

topic: Public speaking
stem: Maintaining eye contact with the audience helps to:
explanation: Eye contact should be distributed across the room.
source: BEU syllabus — Professional Skill Development, Unit 1

topic: Public speaking
stem: Modulation in speech refers to varying:
options: Pitch, pace and volume to keep the delivery interesting
explanation: A monotone delivery quickly loses the audience.
source: BEU syllabus — Professional Skill Development, Unit 1

topic: Public speaking
stem: A pause used effectively in a speech can:
options: Emphasise a point and give the audience time to absorb it
explanation: It is far better than filler words such as um and ah.
source: BEU syllabus — Professional Skill Development, Unit 1

topic: Public speaking
stem: Extemporaneous speaking means speaking:
options: From brief notes after thorough preparation
explanation: It combines preparation with natural delivery.
source: BEU syllabus — Professional Skill Development, Unit 1

topic: Public speaking
stem: Handling a hostile question during a talk is best done by:
options: Listening fully, acknowledging the point and responding calmly with facts
explanation: Composure preserves the speaker's credibility.
source: BEU syllabus — Professional Skill Development, Unit 1

topic: Group discussion
stem: A group discussion in a selection process primarily assesses:
options: Communication, leadership, reasoning and team behaviour
explanation: How you contribute matters as much as what you say.
source: BEU syllabus — Professional Skill Development, Unit 1

topic: Group discussion
stem: Initiating a group discussion is advantageous only if:
options: You have clarity on the topic and can define it well
explanation: A poor start can damage the impression created.
source: BEU syllabus — Professional Skill Development, Unit 1

topic: Group discussion
stem: In a group discussion, disagreeing with another participant should be done:
options: Politely, addressing the idea rather than the person
explanation: Courtesy demonstrates emotional maturity.
source: BEU syllabus — Professional Skill Development, Unit 1

topic: Group discussion
stem: A participant who dominates a group discussion is usually assessed as:
options: Lacking team skills, even if the content is good
explanation: Evaluators look for collaboration, not monopoly.
source: BEU syllabus — Professional Skill Development, Unit 1

topic: Group discussion
stem: Summarising at the end of a group discussion is valuable because it:
options: Shows listening ability and captures the group's consensus
explanation: A good summary should be brief and balanced.
source: BEU syllabus — Professional Skill Development, Unit 1

topic: Group discussion
stem: Active listening in a group discussion involves:
options: Paying attention, noting points and building on others' ideas
explanation: Referring to a previous speaker by name shows engagement.
source: BEU syllabus — Professional Skill Development, Unit 1

topic: Group discussion
stem: A case based group discussion requires participants to:
options: Analyse a situation and propose a justified course of action
explanation: Structured reasoning is valued over rhetoric.
source: BEU syllabus — Professional Skill Development, Unit 1

topic: Group discussion
stem: If a group discussion becomes chaotic, a good participant will:

stem: The fundamental torque equation of a drive is:

stem: Speed control by inserting resistance in the armature circuit is undesirable because it:

stem: The power delivered by a DC motor in the field weakening region is:

source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-II: Electrical Drives [100613], Unit 1

topic: Armature voltage control and flux weakening

source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-II: Electrical Drives [100613], Unit 1

topic: Load torque-speed characteristics and operating point

source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-II: Electrical Drives [100613], Unit 1

stem:

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

Field weakening gives constant power above base speed

stem: The steady state armature current of a chopper fed DC motor equals:

stem: A chopper fed drive with Vs = 220 V and D = 0.5 supplies an average armature voltage of:

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

stem:
Assertion (A): Current limit control gives smooth starting of a DC drive.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

topic: Motoring and generating modes of a separately excited DC machine

topic: Motoring and generating modes of a separately excited DC machine

topic: Motoring and generating modes of a separately excited DC machine

topic: Single, two and four quadrant choppers

stem: A hoist lowering a heavy load with the motor holding it back operates in:

topic: Multi-quadrant chopper fed drive operation and regenerative braking
stem: The maximum regenerative braking torque of a DC drive is limited by:

A is false but R is true

A is false but R is true

topic: Image sampling and quantization
stem: False contouring in a digital image is caused by:
options: Using too few grey levels in a smoothly varying region
explanation: It becomes visible below about 6 bits per pixel.

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Image sampling and quantization
stem: Checkerboard or blocking artefacts appear when an image is:
options: Undersampled spatially, making individual pixels visible
explanation: Spatial resolution is inadequate for the detail present.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Image sampling and quantization
stem: The Nyquist criterion for image sampling requires the sampling rate to be:
options: At least twice the highest spatial frequency present
explanation: Otherwise aliasing occurs.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Image sampling and quantization
stem: Aliasing in a digital image typically appears as:
explanation: An anti-aliasing low pass filter before sampling prevents it.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Image sampling and quantization
stem: Spatial resolution of an image is determined by:
options: The number of pixels per unit distance
explanation: Grey level resolution is determined by the number of bits.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Image sampling and quantization
stem: Dithering or halftoning is used to:
options: Simulate additional grey levels on a display with few levels
explanation: Error diffusion is a common dithering technique.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Image sampling and quantization
stem: Image interpolation methods used in resizing include:
explanation: Bicubic gives the smoothest result at higher computational cost.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Basic relationships between pixels: neighbourhood, adjacency, connectivity and distance measures
stem: The 4-neighbours of a pixel at coordinates x, y are:
options: The two horizontal and two vertical adjacent pixels
explanation: This set is denoted N4 of p.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Basic relationships between pixels: neighbourhood, adjacency, connectivity and distance measures
stem: The 8-neighbourhood of a pixel consists of:
options: Its 4-neighbours together with its four diagonal neighbours
explanation: The diagonal set alone is denoted ND.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Basic relationships between pixels: neighbourhood, adjacency, connectivity and distance measures
stem: Two pixels are said to be 4-adjacent if they are:
options: In each other's 4-neighbourhood and have values from the same set V
explanation: Adjacency requires both spatial proximity and value membership.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Basic relationships between pixels: neighbourhood, adjacency, connectivity and distance measures
stem: Mixed or m-adjacency is introduced to:
options: Eliminate the ambiguity of multiple paths that arises with 8-adjacency
explanation: It gives a unique path between connected pixels.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Basic relationships between pixels: neighbourhood, adjacency, connectivity and distance measures
stem: A digital path from pixel p to pixel q is:
options: A sequence of distinct adjacent pixels beginning at p and ending at q
explanation: Its length is the number of steps in the sequence.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Basic relationships between pixels: neighbourhood, adjacency, connectivity and distance measures
stem: A connected component of an image region is:
options: A maximal set of pixels all connected to each other
explanation: Labelling algorithms identify these components.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Basic relationships between pixels: neighbourhood, adjacency, connectivity and distance measures
stem: The Euclidean distance between pixels p and q is:
explanation: Points within a given Euclidean distance form a disc.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Basic relationships between pixels: neighbourhood, adjacency, connectivity and distance measures
stem: The city block or D4 distance is defined as:
explanation: Points at equal D4 distance form a diamond shape.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Basic relationships between pixels: neighbourhood, adjacency, connectivity and distance measures
stem: The chessboard or D8 distance is defined as:
explanation: Points at equal D8 distance form a square.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Basic relationships between pixels: neighbourhood, adjacency, connectivity and distance measures
stem: The boundary of a region consists of pixels that:
options: Belong to the region and have at least one neighbour outside it
explanation: Inner and outer boundaries can be distinguished.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Basic relationships between pixels: neighbourhood, adjacency, connectivity and distance measures
stem: If 8-connectivity is used for foreground objects, the background should use:
options: 4-connectivity, to satisfy the Jordan curve property
explanation: Mixing them consistently avoids topological paradoxes.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Basic relationships between pixels: neighbourhood, adjacency, connectivity and distance measures
stem: Arithmetic and logical operations between two images require them to:
options: Be of the same size, being performed pixel by pixel
explanation: Image subtraction is widely used for change detection.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Image sampling and quantization
stem: Quantization refers to the digitisation of spatial coordinates.
explanation: Sampling digitises the coordinates; quantization digitises the amplitude.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Basic relationships between pixels: neighbourhood, adjacency, connectivity and distance measures
stem: The city block distance between two pixels equals the sum of the coordinate differences.
explanation: D4 equals the absolute difference in x plus the absolute difference in y.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Basic relationships between pixels: neighbourhood, adjacency, connectivity and distance measures
stem:
Assertion (A): Mixed adjacency is used in digital image analysis.
Reason (R): Pure 8-adjacency can create multiple connection paths between the same pair of pixels.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: m-adjacency removes this ambiguity and yields unique paths.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Image sampling and quantization
stem:
Assertion (A): False contours appear when an image uses too few grey levels.
Reason (R): Smooth intensity gradients are then rendered as discrete visible steps.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The effect becomes obvious below about six bits per pixel.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Basic relationships between pixels: neighbourhood, adjacency, connectivity and distance measures
stem: Which are standard distance measures between pixels?
explanation: Histogram distance compares intensity distributions, not pixel positions.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Gray level transformations, histogram equalization and specification
stem: The negative transformation of an image with L levels is given by:
explanation: It is useful for enhancing white detail in dark regions.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Gray level transformations, histogram equalization and specification
stem: The log transformation of an image is used to:
options: Expand dark pixel values and compress bright ones
explanation: It is used to display Fourier spectra.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Gray level transformations, histogram equalization and specification
stem: The power law or gamma transformation is written as:
explanation: Gamma less than one brightens the image.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Gray level transformations, histogram equalization and specification
stem: The histogram of a digital image plots:
options: The number of pixels at each grey level
explanation: Its shape indicates contrast and brightness characteristics.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Gray level transformations, histogram equalization and specification
stem: Histogram equalization uses which transformation function?
options: The cumulative distribution function of the image histogram
explanation: It spreads intensities to give a nearly uniform histogram.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2
