subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Gray level transformations, histogram equalization and specification
stem: The result of histogram equalization is an image with:
options: Enhanced global contrast and an approximately flat histogram
explanation: It is fully automatic, requiring no parameters.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Gray level transformations, histogram equalization and specification
stem: Histogram specification or matching allows the output image to have:
options: A histogram of a desired specified shape
explanation: It gives more control than plain equalization.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Gray level transformations, histogram equalization and specification
stem: Adaptive or local histogram equalization is preferred when:
options: Contrast enhancement is needed differently in different image regions
explanation: CLAHE limits noise amplification by clipping the histogram.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Gray level transformations, histogram equalization and specification
stem: Bit plane slicing decomposes an image into:
options: Binary images corresponding to each bit of the pixel values
explanation: The higher order planes contain most of the visually significant data.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Pixel domain smoothing and sharpening filters
stem: A spatial averaging or box filter:
options: Blurs the image and reduces random noise
explanation: It is a linear low pass filter.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Pixel domain smoothing and sharpening filters
stem: A Gaussian smoothing filter is preferred over a box filter because it:
options: Gives smoother results with fewer ringing artefacts and is separable
explanation: Its weights decrease smoothly with distance from the centre.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Pixel domain smoothing and sharpening filters
stem: The median filter is an order statistics filter that is especially effective against:
explanation: It preserves edges better than linear averaging.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Pixel domain smoothing and sharpening filters
stem: The max filter is useful for:
options: Removing pepper noise, which consists of dark points
explanation: The min filter removes salt noise instead.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Pixel domain smoothing and sharpening filters
stem: Image sharpening in the spatial domain is achieved using:
options: Derivative operators that emphasise intensity transitions
explanation: Second derivative operators respond strongly to fine detail.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Pixel domain smoothing and sharpening filters
stem: The gradient magnitude of an image is a:
options: First derivative measure used for edge detection
explanation: Sobel masks are the common discrete approximation.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Pixel domain smoothing and sharpening filters
stem: The Laplacian operator is a:
options: Second derivative isotropic operator that highlights fine detail
explanation: It is very sensitive to noise, so smoothing is applied first.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Pixel domain smoothing and sharpening filters
stem: Unsharp masking sharpens an image by:
options: Subtracting a blurred version from the original and adding the difference back
explanation: High boost filtering uses a weighting factor greater than one.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Pixel domain smoothing and sharpening filters
stem: The Sobel operator differs from the Prewitt operator because it:
options: Gives greater weight to the centre pixels, providing some smoothing
explanation: Both are 3 by 3 first derivative masks.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Two dimensional DFT and frequency domain filtering
stem: The two dimensional discrete Fourier transform of an image represents it as:
options: A sum of complex sinusoids of different spatial frequencies
explanation: Its magnitude spectrum shows the frequency content.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Two dimensional DFT and frequency domain filtering
stem: The DC term of the two dimensional DFT of an image corresponds to:
options: The average intensity of the image
explanation: It is usually the largest coefficient in the spectrum.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Two dimensional DFT and frequency domain filtering
stem: High frequency components of an image spectrum correspond to:
explanation: Low frequencies represent slowly varying regions.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Two dimensional DFT and frequency domain filtering
stem: The convolution theorem states that spatial convolution corresponds to:
explanation: This makes large kernel filtering efficient using the FFT.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Two dimensional DFT and frequency domain filtering
stem: An ideal low pass filter in the frequency domain causes:
options: Ringing artefacts because of its abrupt cut-off
explanation: Its spatial equivalent is a sinc-like function with side lobes.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Two dimensional DFT and frequency domain filtering
stem: A Butterworth low pass filter of higher order:
options: Approaches the ideal filter and shows more ringing
explanation: Order one gives a very smooth transition with no ringing.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Two dimensional DFT and frequency domain filtering
stem: A Gaussian low pass filter is attractive because:
options: Its inverse transform is also Gaussian, so there is no ringing
explanation: Both domains show a smooth non-negative function.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Two dimensional DFT and frequency domain filtering
stem: A high pass filter is obtained from a low pass filter by:
options: Subtracting the low pass transfer function from one
explanation: High frequency emphasis adds an offset to preserve the DC term.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Two dimensional DFT and frequency domain filtering
stem: Shifting the origin of the Fourier spectrum to the centre is done by:
options: Multiplying the image by minus one to the power x plus y before transforming
explanation: This makes the spectrum easier to visualise and filter.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Two dimensional DFT and frequency domain filtering
stem: A notch filter in the frequency domain is used to remove:
options: Periodic interference appearing as isolated spectral spikes
explanation: Conjugate symmetric pairs of notches must be applied.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Two dimensional DFT and frequency domain filtering
stem: Zero padding before frequency domain filtering is used to:
options: Avoid wraparound error caused by circular convolution
explanation: The padded size should be at least the sum of the two sizes minus one.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Two dimensional DFT and frequency domain filtering
stem: Homomorphic filtering separates illumination and reflectance by:
options: Taking the logarithm before Fourier filtering and exponentiating afterwards
explanation: It simultaneously compresses dynamic range and enhances contrast.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Pixel domain smoothing and sharpening filters
stem: The median filter is a linear filter.
explanation: It is a non-linear order statistics filter that selects the middle value.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Gray level transformations, histogram equalization and specification
stem: Histogram equalization uses the cumulative distribution function as its transformation.
explanation: Mapping intensities through the normalised CDF gives an approximately uniform histogram.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Two dimensional DFT and frequency domain filtering
stem:
Assertion (A): Ideal low pass filters produce ringing in the filtered image.
Reason (R): An abrupt cut-off in the frequency domain corresponds to a sinc function in the spatial domain.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The sinc side lobes create ripples around sharp edges.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Pixel domain smoothing and sharpening filters
stem:
Assertion (A): The Laplacian is usually applied after smoothing the image.
Reason (R): Second derivative operators strongly amplify high frequency noise.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The Laplacian of Gaussian combines both operations in one kernel.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Pixel domain smoothing and sharpening filters
stem: Which operations sharpen an image?
explanation: Gaussian smoothing is a low pass operation that blurs rather than sharpens.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 2

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color models: RGB, YUV and HSI
stem: The RGB colour model is:
options: An additive model based on the three primary colours of light
explanation: It matches how display devices produce colour.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color models: RGB, YUV and HSI
stem: The CMY model is used for printing because it is:
explanation: CMYK adds black ink for better blacks and cheaper printing.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color models: RGB, YUV and HSI
stem: A 24-bit RGB image can represent how many distinct colours?
explanation: Each of the three channels has 8 bits giving 256 levels.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color models: RGB, YUV and HSI
stem: The HSI colour model separates:
options: Intensity from the colour information of hue and saturation
explanation: This lets grey scale techniques be applied to the intensity channel.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color models: RGB, YUV and HSI
stem: Hue in the HSI model represents:
options: The dominant wavelength or pure colour attribute
explanation: Saturation measures the amount of white mixed with the hue.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color models: RGB, YUV and HSI
stem: The YUV or YCbCr model is widely used in video because:
options: The chrominance channels can be subsampled with little visible loss
explanation: 4:2:0 subsampling halves the chroma resolution in both directions.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color models: RGB, YUV and HSI
stem: The luminance Y in the YUV model is computed as:
options: A weighted sum of R, G and B with the largest weight on green
The average of R, G and B
The maximum of R, G and B
explanation: Y equals about 0.299R plus 0.587G plus 0.114B.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color models: RGB, YUV and HSI
stem: The CIE chromaticity diagram represents:
options: All perceivable colours in terms of two normalised chromaticity coordinates
explanation: A device gamut appears as a triangle inside the horseshoe shape.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color models: RGB, YUV and HSI
stem: The CIE L*a*b* colour space is described as perceptually uniform, meaning:
options: Equal numerical differences correspond to roughly equal perceived differences
explanation: This makes it useful for colour difference measurement.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color transformations, complements, slicing and tone and color corrections
stem: A colour transformation operates on:
options: The component values of each pixel to produce new component values
explanation: It can be applied in any suitable colour space.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color transformations, complements, slicing and tone and color corrections
stem: The colour complement of a pixel corresponds to:
options: The hue diametrically opposite on the colour circle
explanation: In RGB it is obtained by subtracting each component from the maximum.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color transformations, complements, slicing and tone and color corrections
stem: Colour slicing highlights a specific range of colours by:
options: Mapping pixels outside the range of interest to a neutral colour
explanation: A cube or sphere in colour space defines the range.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color transformations, complements, slicing and tone and color corrections
stem: Tone correction of a colour image is usually performed using:
options: A power law or gamma curve applied to the intensity component
explanation: Applying it in RGB can shift hues if not done carefully.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color transformations, complements, slicing and tone and color corrections
stem: Colour balance correction adjusts:
options: The relative strengths of the colour channels to remove a colour cast
explanation: White balancing is a common instance.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color transformations, complements, slicing and tone and color corrections
stem: Histogram equalization of a colour image is best performed on:
options: The intensity channel in HSI, leaving hue and saturation unchanged
explanation: Equalising RGB channels separately distorts the colours.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color transformations, complements, slicing and tone and color corrections
stem: Pseudo-colour or false colour processing assigns:
options: Colours to grey levels of a monochrome image to aid visualisation
explanation: Intensity slicing is the simplest such technique.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color transformations, complements, slicing and tone and color corrections
stem: Gamut mapping is required when:
options: Colours in the source image cannot be reproduced by the destination device
explanation: Out of gamut colours are mapped to the nearest reproducible ones.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color transformations, complements, slicing and tone and color corrections
stem: A colour management system uses ICC profiles to:
options: Convert colours between devices via a device independent connection space
explanation: CIE XYZ or Lab serves as the profile connection space.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color image smoothing, sharpening and segmentation
stem: Smoothing a colour image by averaging can be done by:
options: Applying the averaging mask independently to each RGB component
explanation: This is equivalent to averaging the colour vectors.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color image smoothing, sharpening and segmentation
stem: Applying a scalar median filter independently to each RGB channel can:
options: Produce colours that did not exist in the original image
explanation: Vector median filtering avoids this artefact.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color image smoothing, sharpening and segmentation
stem: Colour image sharpening using the Laplacian is performed by:
options: Computing the Laplacian of each component and combining the results
explanation: Working on the intensity channel of HSI avoids hue shifts.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color image smoothing, sharpening and segmentation
stem: Colour segmentation in the HSI space is often based on:
options: Thresholding the hue channel with a saturation mask
explanation: Hue is relatively invariant to illumination changes.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color image smoothing, sharpening and segmentation
stem: Segmentation in RGB vector space typically uses:
options: A distance measure from a reference colour, forming a sphere or box
explanation: Pixels within the threshold distance are labelled as belonging to the class.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color image smoothing, sharpening and segmentation
stem: Skin colour detection commonly uses:
options: Chrominance components in YCbCr, which cluster tightly for skin
explanation: This makes the detection largely brightness independent.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color image smoothing, sharpening and segmentation
stem: Colour edge detection differs from grey scale edge detection because:
options: Gradients of the three components must be combined into a vector gradient
explanation: Di Zenzo's method computes the vector gradient properly.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color image smoothing, sharpening and segmentation
stem: Noise in a colour image often affects the RGB channels:
explanation: Converting to HSI can concentrate the noise effect in the intensity.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color image smoothing, sharpening and segmentation
stem: Clustering methods such as k-means are used for colour segmentation to:
options: Group pixels with similar colour vectors into a small number of classes
explanation: The number of clusters must be chosen in advance.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color image smoothing, sharpening and segmentation
stem: A drawback of using the hue channel for segmentation is that hue is:
options: Undefined or unstable for low saturation and very dark or bright pixels
explanation: A saturation threshold is normally applied as a mask.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color image smoothing, sharpening and segmentation
stem: Converting RGB to HSI is non-linear, which means that:
options: Filtering in HSI is not equivalent to filtering in RGB
The conversion is lossless in filtering
explanation: Care is needed when choosing the processing space.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color models: RGB, YUV and HSI
stem: Chroma subsampling denoted 4:2:0 means that:
options: The chrominance channels are halved in both horizontal and vertical resolution
explanation: It exploits the eye's lower sensitivity to chroma detail.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color models: RGB, YUV and HSI
stem: The RGB model is a subtractive colour model.
explanation: RGB is additive; CMY and CMYK are the subtractive models used for printing.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color image smoothing, sharpening and segmentation
stem: Applying the median filter separately to each RGB channel can create new colours.
explanation: Independent channel medians may combine into a colour vector absent from the original image.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color models: RGB, YUV and HSI
stem:
Assertion (A): The YCbCr model is preferred to RGB for video compression.
Reason (R): Human vision is much less sensitive to spatial detail in chrominance than in luminance.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Chroma channels can therefore be subsampled with little perceptual loss.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color transformations, complements, slicing and tone and color corrections
stem:
Assertion (A): Histogram equalization of colour images is applied to the intensity channel.
Reason (R): Equalising the R, G and B channels independently changes the relative component ratios.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: That would shift the hues and produce unnatural colours.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Color models: RGB, YUV and HSI
stem: Which are recognised colour models used in image processing?
explanation: The DFT is a frequency domain transform, not a colour model.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 3

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Detection of discontinuities, edge linking and boundary detection
stem: The three basic types of intensity discontinuity in an image are:
explanation: Each is detected with an appropriate mask.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Detection of discontinuities, edge linking and boundary detection
stem: An isolated point in an image is detected using:
options: A Laplacian type mask with a large centre weight and thresholding
explanation: A strong response indicates an isolated bright or dark point.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Detection of discontinuities, edge linking and boundary detection
stem: An ideal step edge in an image produces:
options: A peak in the second derivative
A peak in the first derivative and a zero crossing in the second
explanation: Zero crossings of the Laplacian are used to locate edges.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Detection of discontinuities, edge linking and boundary detection
stem: The Canny edge detector consists of the steps:
options: Gaussian smoothing, gradient computation, non-maximum suppression and hysteresis thresholding
explanation: It is optimal for step edges corrupted by Gaussian noise.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Detection of discontinuities, edge linking and boundary detection
stem: Non-maximum suppression in edge detection is used to:
options: Thin the gradient ridges to single pixel wide edges
explanation: Only local maxima along the gradient direction are kept.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Detection of discontinuities, edge linking and boundary detection
stem: Hysteresis thresholding in Canny edge detection uses:
options: Two thresholds, keeping weak edges only if connected to strong ones
explanation: This reduces broken edges while suppressing noise.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Detection of discontinuities, edge linking and boundary detection
stem: Local edge linking joins edge pixels that have:
options: Similar gradient magnitude and direction within a small neighbourhood
explanation: It builds boundaries from isolated edge points.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Detection of discontinuities, edge linking and boundary detection
stem: The Hough transform detects lines by:
options: Mapping edge points into a parameter space and finding accumulator peaks
explanation: The rho theta parameterisation avoids infinite slopes.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Detection of discontinuities, edge linking and boundary detection
stem: The Laplacian of Gaussian operator is also called the:
explanation: Marr and Hildreth proposed it for edge detection.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Thresholding, global and adaptive, and region based segmentation
stem: Global thresholding segments an image by:
options: Using a single intensity threshold for the entire image
explanation: It works well when the histogram is clearly bimodal.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Thresholding, global and adaptive, and region based segmentation
stem: Otsu's method selects a threshold by:
options: Maximising the between class variance of the two intensity groups
explanation: This is equivalent to minimising the within class variance.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Thresholding, global and adaptive, and region based segmentation
stem: Adaptive or local thresholding is required when:
explanation: A separate threshold is computed for each subregion.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Thresholding, global and adaptive, and region based segmentation
stem: A bimodal histogram indicates that the image contains:
options: Two dominant intensity groups such as object and background
explanation: The valley between the peaks gives a natural threshold.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Thresholding, global and adaptive, and region based segmentation
stem: Region growing segments an image by:
options: Starting from seed pixels and appending similar neighbouring pixels
explanation: The similarity predicate and seed choice determine the result.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Thresholding, global and adaptive, and region based segmentation
stem: The split and merge algorithm uses:
options: A quadtree, splitting non-uniform regions and merging similar adjacent ones
explanation: It avoids the need to choose seed points.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Thresholding, global and adaptive, and region based segmentation
stem: The watershed transform treats an image as:
options: A topographic surface flooded from regional minima
explanation: Marker controlled watershed avoids over-segmentation.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Thresholding, global and adaptive, and region based segmentation
stem: Over-segmentation in the watershed algorithm is caused by:
options: Noise and texture creating many spurious local minima
explanation: Smoothing and marker imposition reduce it.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Thresholding, global and adaptive, and region based segmentation
stem: Segmentation based on region properties differs from edge based methods because it:
explanation: Edge based methods often yield gaps requiring linking.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Wavelets and multi-resolution image processing
stem: The uncertainty principle in signal analysis states that:
options: A signal cannot be arbitrarily localised in both time and frequency simultaneously
explanation: The product of the two spreads has a lower bound.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Wavelets and multi-resolution image processing
stem: A key limitation of the Fourier transform for image analysis is that it:
options: Gives no spatial localisation of frequency content
explanation: Wavelets provide joint space-frequency localisation.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Wavelets and multi-resolution image processing
stem: The short time Fourier transform improves localisation but:
options: Uses a fixed window size, giving the same resolution at all frequencies
explanation: Wavelets instead use scale dependent window widths.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Wavelets and multi-resolution image processing
stem: The continuous wavelet transform correlates a signal with:
options: Scaled and translated versions of a mother wavelet
explanation: Small scales capture fine detail and large scales coarse structure.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Wavelets and multi-resolution image processing
stem: Multi-resolution analysis represents an image as:
options: A coarse approximation plus detail at successively finer scales
explanation: Scaling functions give approximations and wavelets give details.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Wavelets and multi-resolution image processing
stem: One level of two dimensional discrete wavelet decomposition of an image produces:
options: Four subbands: LL, LH, HL and HH
explanation: The LL band is decomposed again at the next level.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Wavelets and multi-resolution image processing
stem: The LL subband of a wavelet decomposition contains:
options: A smoothed, downsampled approximation of the original image
explanation: HL, LH and HH carry the directional detail.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Wavelets and multi-resolution image processing
stem: Wavelet based image compression such as JPEG2000 is effective because:
options: Wavelet coefficients of natural images are sparse, with energy compacted in few coefficients
explanation: It also avoids the blocking artefacts of block DCT coding.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Wavelets and multi-resolution image processing
stem: Wavelet based denoising works by:
options: Thresholding small detail coefficients that mostly represent noise
explanation: Soft and hard thresholding are the two standard rules.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Wavelets and multi-resolution image processing
stem: The Haar wavelet is the simplest wavelet and consists of:
options: A short square shaped function, orthogonal and compactly supported
explanation: Its poor smoothness limits compression performance.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Wavelets and multi-resolution image processing
stem: A filter bank implementation of the discrete wavelet transform uses:
options: Low pass and high pass filters followed by downsampling by two
explanation: Perfect reconstruction requires quadrature mirror filters.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Wavelets and multi-resolution image processing
stem: The number of subbands after a three level dyadic 2D wavelet decomposition is:
explanation: Three detail bands per level plus one final approximation band.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Thresholding, global and adaptive, and region based segmentation
stem: Otsu's method chooses a threshold by maximising the between class variance.
explanation: This is equivalent to minimising the weighted within class variance.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Wavelets and multi-resolution image processing
stem: The Fourier transform provides spatial localisation of frequency content.
explanation: It gives only global frequency information; wavelets provide joint localisation.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Detection of discontinuities, edge linking and boundary detection
stem:
Assertion (A): The Canny detector smooths the image before computing gradients.
Reason (R): Differentiation strongly amplifies high frequency noise.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Gaussian smoothing suppresses the noise while preserving significant edges.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Wavelets and multi-resolution image processing
stem:
Assertion (A): Wavelet transforms are preferred to the DCT in JPEG2000.
Reason (R): The wavelet transform is applied to the whole image rather than to independent blocks.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: This avoids the blocking artefacts typical of block based DCT coding.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

subject_name: Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614]
topic: Detection of discontinuities, edge linking and boundary detection
stem: Which are stages of the Canny edge detection algorithm?
explanation: Histogram equalization is a contrast enhancement step, not part of Canny.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective-I: Digital Image & Video Processing [100614], Unit 4

topic: True value, accuracy, precision and resolution
stem: The true value of a measurand is:
options: The value that would be obtained by a perfect measurement, never exactly known
explanation: In practice it is approximated by a standard of much higher accuracy.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: True value, accuracy, precision and resolution
stem: Accuracy of an instrument refers to:
options: The closeness of a reading to the true value
explanation: It is usually expressed as a percentage of full scale deflection.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: True value, accuracy, precision and resolution
stem: Precision of an instrument is:
options: The degree of agreement among repeated measurements of the same quantity
explanation: An instrument can be precise yet consistently inaccurate.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: True value, accuracy, precision and resolution
stem: An instrument that gives consistently the same wrong reading is:
explanation: A systematic offset is present that calibration can correct.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: True value, accuracy, precision and resolution
stem: Resolution of an instrument is:
options: The smallest change in input that produces a detectable change in output
explanation: For a digital instrument it is one least significant digit.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: True value, accuracy, precision and resolution
stem: A voltmeter with 0.5% accuracy on a 100 V range reading 20 V has a maximum error of:
options: 0.5 V, which is 2.5% of the reading
explanation: Accuracy specified on full scale gives poorer relative accuracy at low readings.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: True value, accuracy, precision and resolution
stem: A 3.5 digit digital multimeter can display a maximum count of:
explanation: The half digit can only show 0 or 1.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: True value, accuracy, precision and resolution
stem: Repeatability of an instrument refers to:
options: Consistency of readings under identical conditions over a short period
explanation: Reproducibility instead applies over long periods and changed conditions.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: True value, accuracy, precision and resolution
stem: Traceability of a measurement means that:
options: It can be linked to national or international standards by an unbroken chain of calibrations
It is recorded in a log
explanation: Each step in the chain has a stated uncertainty.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: True value, accuracy, precision and resolution
stem: Calibration of an instrument involves:
options: Comparing its readings with a standard of higher accuracy
explanation: The result is a calibration curve or correction table.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Drift, hysteresis and dead-band
stem: Drift in an instrument refers to:
options: A gradual change in output over time with no change in the input
explanation: Zero drift shifts the whole calibration curve upward or downward.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Drift, hysteresis and dead-band
stem: Zero drift and sensitivity drift differ in that sensitivity drift:
options: Changes the slope of the calibration curve
explanation: Temperature variation is a common cause of both.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Drift, hysteresis and dead-band
stem: Hysteresis in an instrument means the output depends on:
options: Whether the input is increasing or decreasing
explanation: It arises from friction, backlash and magnetic or elastic memory.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Drift, hysteresis and dead-band
stem: Dead-band or dead zone of an instrument is:
options: The range of input over which the output does not change at all
explanation: Static friction in a mechanical movement is a typical cause.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Drift, hysteresis and dead-band
stem: Threshold of an instrument refers to:
options: The minimum input required to produce a detectable output from zero
explanation: It differs from resolution, which applies at non-zero inputs.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Drift, hysteresis and dead-band
stem: Backlash in a geared instrument mechanism produces:
options: Hysteresis and dead-band on reversal of the input
explanation: Spring loaded anti-backlash gears reduce the effect.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Drift, hysteresis and dead-band
stem: Stability of an instrument refers to its ability to:
options: Retain its calibration over a long period of time
explanation: Periodic recalibration compensates for gradual degradation.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Drift, hysteresis and dead-band
stem: A loading error occurs when an instrument:
options: Draws energy from the measured circuit, altering the quantity being measured
explanation: High input impedance voltmeters minimise this error.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Sensitivity and static characteristics of instruments
stem: Sensitivity of an instrument is defined as:
options: The ratio of change in output to change in input
explanation: It is the slope of the calibration curve.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Sensitivity and static characteristics of instruments
stem: A thermocouple giving 40 microvolts per degree Celsius has a sensitivity of:
explanation: Sensitivity is expressed as output units per input unit.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Sensitivity and static characteristics of instruments
stem: Linearity of an instrument refers to:
options: How closely the calibration curve approaches a straight line
explanation: Nonlinearity is usually specified as a percentage of full scale.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Sensitivity and static characteristics of instruments
stem: The static characteristics of an instrument describe its behaviour when:
options: The measured quantity is constant or changing very slowly
explanation: Dynamic characteristics apply to rapidly varying inputs.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Sensitivity and static characteristics of instruments
stem: The span of an instrument is:
options: The difference between the upper and lower range limits
explanation: A 20 to 100 degree instrument has a span of 80 degrees.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Sensitivity and static characteristics of instruments
stem: A voltmeter's sensitivity is often quoted in ohms per volt, which equals:
options: The reciprocal of the full scale deflection current
explanation: A 20 kilo-ohm per volt meter has a 50 microampere movement.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Sensitivity and static characteristics of instruments
stem: The dynamic characteristics of an instrument include:
options: Speed of response, time constant, settling time and dynamic error
explanation: A first order instrument is characterised by its time constant.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Sensitivity and static characteristics of instruments
stem: Fidelity of an instrument is its ability to:
options: Reproduce a varying input without dynamic distortion
explanation: Dynamic error is the deviation from perfect fidelity.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Sensitivity and static characteristics of instruments
stem: A high input impedance is desirable in a voltmeter because it:
options: Minimises the loading effect on the circuit under test
explanation: Digital voltmeters typically present 10 megohms or more.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Sensitivity and static characteristics of instruments
stem: An ammeter should have very low resistance because:
options: It is connected in series and must not alter the circuit current
explanation: A shunt of very small resistance extends its range.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Sensitivity and static characteristics of instruments
stem: The time constant of a first order thermometer determines:
options: How quickly it responds to a step change in temperature
explanation: It reaches 63.2% of the final value in one time constant.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: True value, accuracy, precision and resolution
stem: Significant figures in a measurement result convey:
options: Information about the precision of the measurement
explanation: Reporting more digits than justified misrepresents the precision.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: True value, accuracy, precision and resolution
stem: An instrument can be precise without being accurate.
explanation: Repeatable readings can still be consistently offset from the true value.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Drift, hysteresis and dead-band
stem: Hysteresis causes an instrument to give different readings for increasing and decreasing inputs.
explanation: Friction, backlash and material memory are the usual causes.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Sensitivity and static characteristics of instruments
stem:
Assertion (A): Voltmeters are designed with very high input resistance.
Reason (R): A low resistance voltmeter would draw current and change the voltage it is measuring.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Minimising this loading error is essential for accurate voltage measurement.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: True value, accuracy, precision and resolution
stem:
Assertion (A): Accuracy specified as a percentage of full scale gives poorer relative accuracy at low readings.
Reason (R): The absolute error stays constant while the reading itself becomes smaller.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Instruments should therefore be operated in the upper part of their range.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Drift, hysteresis and dead-band
stem: Which are static characteristics of a measuring instrument?
explanation: Time constant is a dynamic characteristic describing the speed of response.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 1

topic: Types of errors in measurements
stem: Errors in measurement are broadly classified as:
explanation: Each class demands a different remedial approach.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Types of errors in measurements
stem: Gross errors are caused mainly by:
options: Human mistakes in reading, recording or computing
explanation: Careful technique and repeated readings by different observers reduce them.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Types of errors in measurements
stem: Systematic errors are characterised by:
options: A consistent bias in one direction that can in principle be corrected
explanation: Calibration against a standard removes most of them.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Types of errors in measurements
stem: Instrumental errors arise from:
options: Inherent shortcomings of the instrument such as friction and wear
explanation: They include loading effects and calibration errors.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Types of errors in measurements
stem: Environmental errors are caused by:
options: Changes in temperature, humidity, pressure or magnetic fields
explanation: Shielding, air conditioning and correction factors mitigate them.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Types of errors in measurements
stem: Parallax error in reading an analogue meter is classified as:
explanation: A mirror behind the pointer scale eliminates it.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Types of errors in measurements
stem: Random errors are best reduced by:
options: Taking many readings and computing the average
explanation: They obey a normal distribution about the mean.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Types of errors in measurements
stem: Absolute error is defined as:
options: The difference between the measured and true values
explanation: Relative error expresses it as a fraction of the true value.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Types of errors in measurements
stem: When two quantities with errors are added, the resultant absolute errors:
options: Add directly in the worst case
explanation: For products and quotients, relative errors add instead.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Types of errors in measurements
stem: For a quantity computed as the product of two measurements, the relative error is approximately:
options: The sum of the individual relative errors
explanation: For a power x^n the relative error is multiplied by n.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Statistical analysis: mean, standard deviation and probable error
stem: The arithmetic mean of a set of readings is the best estimate of the true value when:
explanation: Random errors are equally likely to be positive or negative.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Statistical analysis: mean, standard deviation and probable error
stem: The deviation of a reading is defined as:
options: The reading minus the true value
The reading minus the arithmetic mean
explanation: The algebraic sum of all deviations from the mean is zero.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Statistical analysis: mean, standard deviation and probable error
stem: The standard deviation of a set of measurements indicates:
options: The dispersion or spread of the readings about the mean
explanation: A small standard deviation implies high precision.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Statistical analysis: mean, standard deviation and probable error
stem: For a normal distribution, the fraction of readings within plus or minus one standard deviation is:
explanation: Two sigma covers 95.5% and three sigma 99.7%.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Statistical analysis: mean, standard deviation and probable error
stem: The probable error of a single reading is:
explanation: Half the readings lie within plus or minus the probable error.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Statistical analysis: mean, standard deviation and probable error
stem: The standard deviation of the mean of n readings is:
options: Sigma divided by the square root of n
explanation: Averaging more readings improves the estimate of the mean.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Statistical analysis: mean, standard deviation and probable error
stem: The variance of a set of readings is:
options: The square of the standard deviation
explanation: Variances of independent error sources add directly.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Statistical analysis: mean, standard deviation and probable error
stem: A Gaussian or normal error curve is:
options: Symmetrical and bell shaped about the mean
explanation: Small errors are far more likely than large ones.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Statistical analysis: mean, standard deviation and probable error
stem: Chauvenet's criterion is used to:
options: Decide whether a suspiciously deviating reading should be rejected
explanation: It compares the deviation with a tabulated ratio depending on sample size.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Statistical analysis: mean, standard deviation and probable error
stem: The method of least squares is used in measurement analysis to:
options: Fit the best straight line or curve to a set of experimental data
explanation: It minimises the sum of the squares of the residuals.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Six-sigma estimation, Cp and Cpk process capability indices
stem: Six sigma as a quality methodology aims for a defect rate of:
explanation: It allows for a 1.5 sigma long term process shift.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Six-sigma estimation, Cp and Cpk process capability indices
stem: A six sigma process means the specification limits are located at:
options: Six standard deviations from the process mean
explanation: This gives a very large margin against random variation.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Six-sigma estimation, Cp and Cpk process capability indices
stem: The process capability index Cp is defined as:
options: The specification width divided by six sigma
explanation: Cp assumes the process is perfectly centred.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Six-sigma estimation, Cp and Cpk process capability indices
stem: A process with Cp equal to 1.0 has a specification width equal to:
explanation: This corresponds to about 2700 defects per million if centred.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Six-sigma estimation, Cp and Cpk process capability indices
stem: Cpk differs from Cp because Cpk:
options: Accounts for how far the process mean is off centre
explanation: Cpk equals Cp only when the process is perfectly centred.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Six-sigma estimation, Cp and Cpk process capability indices
stem: A Cpk value less than 1 indicates that the process:
options: Is producing output beyond at least one specification limit
explanation: Cpk of 1.33 or more is a common industrial minimum requirement.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Six-sigma estimation, Cp and Cpk process capability indices
stem: If Cp is 2.0 but Cpk is 1.0, the process is:
options: Inherently capable but significantly off centre
explanation: Re-centring the mean would restore Cpk towards Cp.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Six-sigma estimation, Cp and Cpk process capability indices
stem: The DMAIC cycle in six sigma stands for:
options: Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve and Control
explanation: It is the standard improvement roadmap for existing processes.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Six-sigma estimation, Cp and Cpk process capability indices
stem: A control chart in statistical process control is used to:
options: Distinguish common cause variation from special cause variation over time
explanation: Control limits are typically set at plus or minus three sigma.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Six-sigma estimation, Cp and Cpk process capability indices
stem: Process capability indices are valid only if the process is:
options: In statistical control and approximately normally distributed
explanation: Otherwise the computed indices are misleading.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Types of errors in measurements
stem: Random errors can be reduced by taking the average of many readings.
explanation: They are equally likely to be positive or negative, so they tend to cancel.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Six-sigma estimation, Cp and Cpk process capability indices
stem: Cp and Cpk are equal when the process is perfectly centred.
explanation: Cpk penalises only the offset of the mean from the specification centre.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Types of errors in measurements
stem:
Assertion (A): Calibration cannot eliminate random errors.
Reason (R): Random errors vary unpredictably in magnitude and sign from reading to reading.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Only systematic errors have a fixed pattern that calibration can correct.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Statistical analysis: mean, standard deviation and probable error
stem:
Assertion (A): The standard deviation of the mean falls as more readings are taken.
Reason (R): It equals the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Quadrupling the number of readings halves the uncertainty in the mean.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Types of errors in measurements
stem: Which of the following are systematic errors?
explanation: Thermal noise is inherently random and cannot be corrected by calibration.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 2

topic: Temperature and pressure sensors
stem: A transducer is a device that:
options: Converts one form of energy or physical quantity into another, usually electrical
explanation: A sensor is the element that responds directly to the measurand.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Temperature and pressure sensors
stem: A thermocouple generates an EMF based on:
options: The Seebeck effect at a junction of two dissimilar metals
explanation: The EMF depends on the temperature difference between hot and cold junctions.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Temperature and pressure sensors
stem: Cold junction compensation in a thermocouple circuit is needed because:
options: The output depends on the difference between measuring and reference junctions
explanation: Modern instruments measure the terminal temperature electronically.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Temperature and pressure sensors
stem: A platinum resistance thermometer (RTD) works on the principle that:
options: Metal resistance increases almost linearly with temperature
explanation: Pt100 has a resistance of 100 ohms at 0 degrees Celsius.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Temperature and pressure sensors
stem: An NTC thermistor differs from an RTD because its resistance:
options: Decreases sharply and nonlinearly with rising temperature
explanation: Its high sensitivity suits narrow range measurements.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Temperature and pressure sensors
stem: A three wire connection is used with an RTD to:
options: Compensate for the resistance of the connecting lead wires
explanation: A four wire Kelvin connection gives even better accuracy.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Temperature and pressure sensors
stem: A Bourdon tube pressure gauge operates by:
options: Elastic deformation of a curved flattened tube under internal pressure
explanation: The tip motion is amplified by a link and gear sector to a pointer.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Temperature and pressure sensors
stem: A piezoelectric pressure transducer is best suited for measuring:
explanation: Charge leakage prevents it from holding a static reading.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Temperature and pressure sensors
stem: A capacitive pressure sensor detects pressure by:
options: Measuring diaphragm deflection as a change in plate separation
explanation: It offers high sensitivity and low temperature dependence.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Temperature and pressure sensors
stem: A Pirani gauge measures low pressure by sensing:
options: The change in thermal conductivity of the gas via a heated filament
explanation: Ionisation gauges are used for even lower vacuum ranges.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Torque and flow measurement
stem: Torque on a rotating shaft is commonly measured using:
options: Strain gauges bonded at 45 degrees to the shaft axis in a bridge
explanation: Slip rings or telemetry carry the bridge signal off the rotating shaft.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Torque and flow measurement
stem: A strain gauge works on the principle that conductor resistance changes with:
options: Mechanical strain altering its length and cross section
explanation: The gauge factor relates fractional resistance change to strain.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Torque and flow measurement
stem: A four active arm Wheatstone bridge of strain gauges provides:
options: Maximum sensitivity and inherent temperature compensation
explanation: Gauges in adjacent arms experience opposite strains.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Torque and flow measurement
stem: An orifice plate flow meter measures flow by relating flow rate to:
options: The square root of the differential pressure across the restriction
explanation: It is simple and cheap but incurs a permanent pressure loss.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Torque and flow measurement
stem: A venturi meter is preferred over an orifice plate when:
options: Permanent pressure loss must be minimised
explanation: Its gradual convergent-divergent profile recovers most of the pressure.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Torque and flow measurement
stem: An electromagnetic flow meter can be used only with fluids that are:
explanation: It works on Faraday's law with no obstruction to flow.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Torque and flow measurement
stem: A rotameter measures flow using:
options: A float in a tapered vertical tube whose position indicates the rate
explanation: It is a variable area, constant pressure drop device.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Torque and flow measurement
stem: A turbine flow meter produces an output that is:
options: A pulse frequency proportional to the volumetric flow rate
explanation: A magnetic pickup senses the passing rotor blades.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Torque and flow measurement
stem: A Coriolis mass flow meter directly measures:
options: Mass flow rate, independent of fluid density and viscosity
explanation: Vibrating tubes twist in proportion to the mass flow.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Torque and flow measurement
stem: An ultrasonic transit time flow meter determines velocity from:
options: The difference in travel time of pulses sent upstream and downstream
explanation: Clamp-on versions require no pipe penetration at all.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Speed and position sensors
stem: An LVDT measures linear displacement by producing:
options: A differential AC output whose amplitude and phase indicate core position
explanation: It is frictionless and has essentially infinite resolution.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Speed and position sensors
stem: The output of an LVDT at the null position is:
options: Ideally zero, with a small residual voltage in practice
explanation: The phase of the output reverses on either side of null.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Speed and position sensors
stem: An RVDT is used to measure:
options: Angular displacement over a limited range, typically plus or minus 40 degrees
explanation: It works on the same differential transformer principle as the LVDT.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Speed and position sensors
stem: A digital tachometer commonly measures shaft speed by:
options: Counting pulses from a toothed wheel or optical disc in a fixed time
explanation: Accuracy improves with more pulses per revolution.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Speed and position sensors
stem: A stroboscope measures rotational speed by:
options: Flashing at a rate that makes the rotating object appear stationary
explanation: Care is needed to avoid reading a submultiple of the true speed.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Speed and position sensors
stem: An absolute optical encoder differs from an incremental one because it:
options: Outputs a unique code for each shaft position, retained after power loss
explanation: Gray coding avoids ambiguous transitions between adjacent codes.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Speed and position sensors
stem: A proximity sensor of the inductive type detects:
options: The presence of a nearby metallic object without contact
explanation: Capacitive types can also detect non-metallic objects.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Speed and position sensors
stem: A resolver provides shaft angle information as:
options: Sine and cosine modulated output windings
explanation: A resolver to digital converter produces the digital angle.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Speed and position sensors
stem: A piezoelectric accelerometer measures acceleration by sensing:
options: The force exerted by a seismic mass on a piezoelectric crystal
explanation: A charge amplifier converts the charge output into a voltage.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Temperature and pressure sensors
stem: A pyrometer is used for temperature measurement when:
options: The target is very hot or inaccessible, requiring non-contact sensing
explanation: It infers temperature from emitted thermal radiation.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Temperature and pressure sensors
stem: A thermocouple requires an external excitation supply to operate.
explanation: It is self generating, producing an EMF from the Seebeck effect.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Speed and position sensors
stem: An LVDT output phase reverses as the core passes through the null position.
explanation: This phase reversal indicates the direction of displacement.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Torque and flow measurement
stem:
Assertion (A): Orifice plate flow meters have a nonlinear calibration.
Reason (R): Flow rate is proportional to the square root of the differential pressure.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A square root extractor is used to linearise the transmitted signal.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Temperature and pressure sensors
stem:
Assertion (A): RTDs are preferred over thermocouples for accurate moderate temperature measurement.
Reason (R): Platinum resistance varies almost linearly and very repeatably with temperature.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Thermocouples cover a wider range but with lower accuracy and stability.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Torque and flow measurement
stem: Which flow meters cause negligible permanent pressure loss?
explanation: An orifice plate creates a substantial and permanent pressure drop.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 3

topic: Current and voltage measurement, shunts and potential dividers
stem: An ammeter is always connected:
options: In series with the circuit whose current is to be measured
explanation: Its resistance must be as low as possible.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 4

topic: Current and voltage measurement, shunts and potential dividers
stem: A voltmeter is always connected:
options: In parallel across the two points whose potential difference is required
explanation: Its resistance must be as high as possible.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 4

topic: Current and voltage measurement, shunts and potential dividers
stem: A shunt is used with a moving coil movement to:
options: Extend the current range by carrying most of the current
explanation: It is a low resistance connected in parallel with the movement.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 4

topic: Current and voltage measurement, shunts and potential dividers
stem: For a multiplying power of n, the shunt resistance required is:
explanation: Rm is the meter movement resistance.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 4

topic: Current and voltage measurement, shunts and potential dividers
stem: A multiplier resistance in a voltmeter is:
options: A high resistance connected in series with the movement
explanation: The multiplier value is Rm(n-1) for a range multiplication of n.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 4

topic: Current and voltage measurement, shunts and potential dividers
stem: A moving coil (PMMC) instrument can directly measure:
options: DC quantities only, because it responds to the average value
explanation: A rectifier must be added for AC measurement.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 4

topic: Current and voltage measurement, shunts and potential dividers
stem: A moving iron instrument can measure both AC and DC because its deflection is:
options: Proportional to the square of the current, independent of polarity
explanation: Its scale is therefore non-uniform and crowded at the low end.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 4

topic: Current and voltage measurement, shunts and potential dividers
stem: A potential divider used for voltage measurement should:
options: Draw negligible current compared with the circuit under test
explanation: Otherwise it loads the source and distorts the reading.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 4

topic: Current and voltage measurement, shunts and potential dividers
stem: A four terminal (Kelvin) shunt is used because it:
options: Separates the current carrying and potential sensing connections
explanation: Contact and lead resistances are then excluded from the measurement.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 4

topic: Current and voltage measurement, shunts and potential dividers
stem: Manganin is used for shunt resistors because it has:
options: A very low temperature coefficient of resistance
explanation: Its thermo-EMF against copper is also very small.
source: BEU syllabus — Measurements and Instrumentation, Unit 4

topic: Current and voltage measurement, shunts and potential dividers
